### Article 11: Technical Documentation

1. The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date. The technical documentation shall be drawn up in such a way as to demonstrate that the high-risk AI system complies with the requirements set out in this Section and to provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the necessary information in a clear and comprehensive form to assess the compliance of the AI system with those requirements. It shall contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV. SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner. To that end, the Commission shall establish a simplified technical documentation form targeted at the needs of small and microenterprises. Where an SME, including a start-up, opts to provide the information required in Annex IV in a simplified manner, it shall use the form referred to in this paragraph. Notified bodies shall accept the form for the purposes of the conformity assessment.

2. Where a high-risk AI system related to a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I is placed on the market or put into service, a single set of technical documentation shall be drawn up containing all the information set out in paragraph 1, as well as the information required under those legal acts.

3. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend Annex IV, where necessary, to ensure that, in light of technical progress, the technical documentation provides all the information necessary to assess the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in this Section.

**Article 12: Record-Keeping**
### Article 12: Record-Keeping

1. High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

2. In order to ensure a level of traceability of the functioning of a high-risk AI system that is appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for:

(a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification;

(b) facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72; and

(c) monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5).

3. For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1 (a), of Annex III, the logging capabilities shall provide, at a minimum:

(a) recording of the period of each use of the system (start date and time and end date and time of each use);

(b) the reference database against which input data has been checked by the system;

(c) the input data for which the search has led to a match;

(d) the identification of the natural persons involved in the verification of the results, as referred to in Article 14(5).

**Article 19: Automatically Generated Logs**
### Article 19: Automatically Generated Logs

1. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent such logs are under their control. Without prejudice to applicable Union or national law, the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.

2. Providers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law shall maintain the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law.

---

## Comparison: SR 11-7 vs. NIST AI RMF MEASURE Function — Ongoing Performance Monitoring of Production Models

### 1. Core Philosophy & Scope

| Dimension | SR 11-7 (Federal Reserve) | NIST AI RMF MEASURE Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary objective** | Ensure models "perform as expected" relative to business objectives; identify deterioration so that adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment can occur (SR 11-7, §V) | Employ quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools to "analyze, assess, benchmark, and monitor AI risk and related impacts" (AI RMF 1.0, p. 28) |
| **Scope of monitoring** | Focused on model output accuracy, reliability, and fitness-for-purpose in the context of financial risk | Broader: functionality, trustworthiness characteristics (fairness, security, transparency, accountability), social impact, and human-AI configurations |
| **Risk framing** | Model risk as a subset of operational/financial risk; emphasis on "model deterioration" and "acceptable performance ranges" | AI risk as socio-technical; emphasis on trustworthiness tradeoffs, affected communities, and emergent risks |

### 2. Monitoring Triggers & Frequency

**SR 11-7** ties monitoring frequency to model materiality, methodology, and rate of environmental change. It emphasizes that "the frequency and scope of ongoing monitoring" should reflect potential changes in "products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions" (§V, Ongoing Model Monitoring). When "performance deviates meaningfully from expectations," organizations must consider "model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment."

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE** is more prescriptive about *what* to monitor continuously. MEASURE 2.4 requires that "the functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components — as identified in the MAP function — are monitored when in production." The GAI-specific sub-actions go further: MS-1.1-006 calls for "continuous monitoring of GAI system impacts to identify whether GAI outputs are equitable across various sub-populations," and MG-3.2-006 requires "real-time monitoring processes for analyzing generated content performance and trustworthiness characteristics... to identify deviations from the desired standards and trigger alerts for human intervention."

**Key difference:** SR 11-7 leaves frequency to the bank's judgment based on risk; NIST explicitly calls for *continuous* and *real-time* monitoring for certain AI risks.

### 3. Metrics & Measurement Approaches

**SR 11-7** centers on **outcomes analysis**: "compares model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes to assess model performance relative to model objectives and business use" (§V). This includes back-testing, outlier analysis, and developmental testing. The focus is predominantly quantitative and tied to business metrics.

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE** takes a more expansive approach across four subcategories:

- **MEASURE 1.1**: Select metrics for AI risks starting with the most significant; document risks that *cannot* be measured and why (MS-1.1-009).
- **MEASURE 1.2**: "Appropriateness of AI metrics and effectiveness of existing controls are regularly assessed and updated, including reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities."
- **MEASURE 2.3**: Performance/assurance criteria measured "qualitatively or quantitatively" under deployment-like conditions.
- **MEASURE 4.3**: "Measurable performance improvements or declines based on consultations with relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics are identified and documented."

**Key difference:** SR 11-7 is almost exclusively quantitative and business-outcome-focused. NIST explicitly embraces qualitative methods, requires documenting *unmeasurable* risks, and mandates disaggregation of metrics by demographic factors (MS-1.1-003).

### 4. Independent Review & Effective Challenge

**SR 11-7** makes "effective challenge" a cornerstone: "critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring." These individuals must have "appropriate expertise," "sufficient independence to maintain objectivity," and "organizational standing and influence to effect any change" (§III).

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE 1.3** mirrors this: "Internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors are involved in regular assessments and updates." It goes further by requiring consultation with "domain experts, users, AI actors external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system, and affected communities." The GAI profile (MS-1.3-003) explicitly requires verifying that those conducting evaluations "are not directly involved in system development tasks for the same GAI model."

**Key difference:** Both require independence, but NIST extends the circle of reviewers beyond internal experts to include *external* AI actors and *affected communities* — a broader stakeholder model than SR 11-7's "objective experts."

### 5. Documentation & Traceability

**SR 11-7** requires a "comprehensive set of information for models under development or in use" in a model inventory, and "adequate documentation" to support continuity, tracking of recommendations, responses, exceptions, and remediation (§VI).

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE** is more granular: MEASURE 2.1 requires that "test sets, metrics, and details about the tools used during TEVV are documented." MEASURE 4.2 requires that "measurement results regarding AI system trustworthiness in deployment context(s) and across the AI lifecycle are informed by input from domain experts and relevant AI actors to validate whether the system is performing consistently as intended. Results are documented."

**Key difference:** Both require documentation, but NIST emphasizes documentation of the *measurement apparatus itself* (tools, test sets, methods) and validation of results through stakeholder input, not just documentation of outcomes.

### 6. Feedback Loops & User Input

**SR 11-7** acknowledges that "user feedback provides business insights that enhance future development" and that "constructive engagement, particularly around model design, assumptions, and outcomes, strengthens both model understanding and model quality" (§IV). However, this is framed as a development-phase benefit rather than a structured ongoing monitoring mechanism.

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE** institutionalizes feedback far more deeply:

- **MEASURE 3.3**: "Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes are established and integrated into AI system evaluation metrics."
- **MEASURE 4.1**: Measurement approaches are "connected to deployment context(s) and informed through consultation with domain experts and other end users."
- **MANAGE 4.1**: Post-deployment monitoring includes "mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management."

**Key difference:** SR 11-7 treats user feedback as beneficial but ancillary. NIST makes structured feedback from users and affected communities an *integral component* of the measurement system itself, with formal appeal and override mechanisms.

### 7. Security & Resilience Monitoring

**SR 11-7** does not explicitly address security monitoring of models in production. Its focus is on conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis, and performance deterioration.

**NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.7** dedicates an entire subcategory to this: "AI system security and resilience — as identified in the MAP function — are evaluated and documented." This includes red-teaming (MS-2.7-007), benchmarking security against industry standards (MS-2.7-002), measuring reliability of content authentication methods (MS-2.7-005), and regularly verifying that "security measures remain effective and have not been compromised" (MS-2.7-009).

**Key difference:** This is a significant gap in SR 11-7 relative to NIST. SR 11-7 was written before adversarial AI risks were prominent and contains no equivalent to NIST's security and resilience measurement requirements.

### 8. Third-Party / Vendor Models

**SR 11-7** addresses vendor models in §VII: "Sound practice involves conducting ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to assess whether vendor models are accurate, remain fit for purpose, and continue to be reliable." It acknowledges the challenge of proprietary components limiting visibility.

**NIST AI RMF** addresses third-party monitoring across multiple functions: MANAGE 3.1 requires that "AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented." MANAGE 3.2 requires that "pre-trained models which are used for development are monitored as part of AI system regular monitoring and maintenance." The GAI profile adds specific actions for real-time monitoring of third-party generated content (MG-3.2-006) and documentation of how pre-trained models have been adapted (MG-3.2-002).

**Key difference:** Both require third-party monitoring, but NIST is more detailed about *what* to monitor (content filters, adaptation documentation, real-time performance) and extends monitoring to the supply chain and pre-trained model components.

---

## Summary Table

| Monitoring Element | SR 11-7 | NIST AI RMF MEASURE |
|---|---|---|
| Performance metrics | Quantitative, business-outcome focused | Quantitative + qualitative; trustworthiness, fairness, security |
| Monitoring frequency | Risk-based, periodic | Continuous / real-time for key risks |
| Independent review | Effective challenge by objective internal experts | Internal + external experts + affected communities |
| Documentation | Model inventory, outcomes, recommendations | Tools, test sets, metrics, stakeholder validation |
| User feedback | Beneficial but informal | Structured, integrated into metrics; appeal/override mechanisms |
| Security monitoring | Not addressed | Dedicated subcategory (MEASURE 2.7); red-teaming, benchmarks |
| Third-party monitoring | Outcomes analysis; fit-for-purpose | Supply chain, pre-trained models, content filters, real-time alerts |
| Unmeasurable risks | Not explicitly addressed | Must be documented with explanations (MS-1.1-009) |
| Decommissioning triggers | Performance outside thresholds → adjustment/redevelopment | MANAGE 2.4: supersede/disengage systems with outcomes inconsistent with intended use |

---

**Bottom line:** SR 11-7 provides a rigorous but narrower framework centered on quantitative outcomes analysis and effective challenge for financial model risk. NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function is broader in scope — adding security, fairness, transparency, qualitative methods, community feedback, and continuous monitoring — and is designed for the socio-technical risks unique to AI systems. A bank implementing both frameworks would find SR 11-7's outcomes-analysis discipline complementary to NIST's broader trustworthiness measurement, but would need to supplement SR 11-7 with explicit security monitoring, fairness metrics, and structured feedback mechanisms to satisfy the MEASURE function.

## HHS 2024 NPRM: Proposed Changes to the HIPAA Security Rule vs. the 2013 Omnibus Rule Baseline

On **December 27, 2024**, HHS/OCR issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) (published in the Federal Register on January 6, 2025) to significantly overhaul the HIPAA Security Rule — the first major update since the 2013 Omnibus Rule. Below is a structured comparison of the key proposed changes against the 2013 baseline.

---

### 1. ELIMINATION OF "ADDRESSABLE" VS. "REQUIRED" DISTINCTION

**2013 Omnibus Rule baseline:** The Security Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.308, 164.310, 164.312) distinguishes between "Required" and "Addressable" implementation specifications. Under § 164.306(d)(3), addressable specifications allow entities to assess whether a safeguard is "reasonable and appropriate" and either implement it, implement an equivalent alternative, or document why it is not applicable.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **All implementation specifications become mandatory.** The "addressable" designation is eliminated entirely. This means controls that were previously addressable — including encryption and decryption (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv)), automatic logoff (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iii)), transmission security encryption (§ 164.312(e)(2)(ii)), and many administrative safeguards — would become required with only narrow, documented exceptions.

---

### 2. ENCRYPTION — FROM ADDRESSABLE TO MANDATORY

**2013 baseline:** Encryption at rest (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv)) and encryption in transit (§ 164.312(e)(2)(ii)) are both **addressable**. Entities could choose not to encrypt if they documented an equivalent alternative.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit becomes mandatory**, with only limited, documented exceptions. This is one of the most significant shifts, directly converting two addressable specifications into hard requirements.

---

### 3. MULTI-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (MFA)

**2013 baseline:** The Security Rule does not explicitly mention multi-factor authentication. The person or entity authentication standard (§ 164.312(d)) requires entities to "verify that a person or entity seeking access to ePHI is the one claimed" but does not prescribe MFA.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **MFA becomes mandatory** for access to systems handling ePHI, with limited exceptions. This is an entirely new explicit requirement.

---

### 4. NETWORK SEGMENTATION

**2013 baseline:** Not explicitly required. The access control standard (§ 164.312(a)(1)) requires limiting access to authorized persons/programs but does not mandate network segmentation.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Network segmentation is explicitly required** to limit access and prevent lateral movement by attackers within systems containing ePHI.

---

### 5. TECHNOLOGY ASSET INVENTORY & NETWORK MAP

**2013 baseline:** No explicit requirement for a technology asset inventory or network map.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** Covered entities and business associates must **develop and maintain a written technology asset inventory and a network map** illustrating ePHI movement through electronic information systems. This must be reviewed and updated **at least every 12 months** and in response to changes in the environment or operations that may affect ePHI.

---

### 6. MORE PRESCRIPTIVE RISK ANALYSIS

**2013 baseline:** § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) requires an "accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI." The rule does not specify what the written assessment must contain.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** The risk analysis must be a **written assessment** containing specific, enumerated elements (e.g., identification of threats and vulnerabilities, assessment of current security measures, determination of risk levels). This codifies much more granular documentation requirements.

---

### 7. VULNERABILITY SCANNING & PENETRATION TESTING

**2013 baseline:** Not explicitly required. The security management process (§ 164.308(a)(1)) requires risk analysis and risk management but does not mandate specific technical testing.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Vulnerability scanning at least every six months** and **annual penetration testing** become mandatory. This introduces a cadence-based technical testing requirement that did not previously exist.

---

### 8. INCIDENT RESPONSE PLAN — WRITTEN & TESTED

**2013 baseline:** § 164.308(a)(6) requires policies and procedures to "identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents; mitigate, to the extent practicable, harmful effects; and document security incidents and their outcomes." There is no requirement for a formal written incident response plan or regular testing.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** Entities must establish a **written incident response plan** that is **tested and revised at least every 12 months**, with documentation of responses to known or suspected security incidents.

---

### 9. CONTINGENCY PLANNING — 72-HOUR RESTORATION & CRITICALITY ANALYSIS

**2013 baseline:** § 164.308(a)(7) requires a contingency plan with a data backup plan (Required) and disaster recovery plan (Required), but does not specify restoration timelines or require a criticality analysis.

**2024 NPRM proposal:**
- **Written procedures to restore critical relevant electronic information systems and data within 72 hours** of loss of functionality.
- **Perform an analysis of the relative criticality** of systems and data to determine restoration priorities.
- Restoration of non-critical systems in accordance with the criticality analysis.

---

### 10. ANNUAL COMPLIANCE AUDITS

**2013 baseline:** No explicit requirement for periodic compliance audits. The rule requires policies and procedures (§ 164.316) and periodic review of records, but not a formal annual compliance audit.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** Covered entities must **conduct formal compliance audits at least once every 12 months** to verify adherence to Security Rule requirements.

---

### 11. BUSINESS ASSOCIATE VERIFICATION

**2013 baseline:** Business associates must comply with the Security Rule (§ 164.306(a)), and covered entities must have business associate agreements (§ 164.308(b)), but there is no requirement for annual verification of business associate technical safeguards.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Business associates must verify their technical safeguards at least annually**, and covered entities must obtain verification that business associates have implemented required safeguards. This strengthens supply-chain assurance.

---

### 12. CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT & ANTI-MALWARE

**2013 baseline:** Protection from malicious software is an addressable implementation specification (§ 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B)). Configuration management is not explicitly mentioned.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Deployment of anti-malware protection becomes mandatory.** Additionally, **configuration management** and **removal of extraneous software** from electronic information systems are explicitly required.

---

### 13. AUDIT LOGGING

**2013 baseline:** § 164.312(b) requires audit controls — "hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use ePHI" — but does not specify automation.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Automated audit logging** is explicitly required, strengthening the existing audit controls standard.

---

### 14. 24-HOUR WORKFORCE ACCESS TERMINATION NOTIFICATION

**2013 baseline:** Termination procedures (§ 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(C)) are addressable and do not specify a notification timeline.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** **Notification within 24 hours** when a workforce member's access to ePHI or certain electronic information systems is changed or terminated.

---

### 15. WRITTEN DOCUMENTATION FOR ALL POLICIES, PROCEDURES, PLANS & ANALYSES

**2013 baseline:** § 164.316 requires retention of documentation for six years but does not explicitly require that all policies, procedures, plans, and analyses be in written form.

**2024 NPRM proposal:** Entities must **maintain written documentation of all policies, procedures, plans, and analyses** required by the Security Rule, strengthening documentation requirements across the board.

---

### Summary Table

| Area | 2013 Omnibus Rule | 2024 NPRM Proposal |
|------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Addressable vs. Required | Two-tier system | All mandatory |
| Encryption (at rest & in transit) | Addressable | Mandatory |
| MFA | Not specified | Mandatory |
| Network segmentation | Not specified | Mandatory |
| Asset inventory & network map | Not required | Required, updated annually |
| Risk analysis detail | General requirement | Specific written elements |
| Vulnerability scanning | Not specified | Every 6 months |
| Penetration testing | Not specified | Annually |
| Incident response plan | General policies | Written, tested annually |
| Restoration timeline | Not specified | 72 hours for critical systems |
| Compliance audits | Not specified | Annually |
| BA verification | Not specified | Annual verification |
| Anti-malware | Addressable | Mandatory |
| Configuration management | Not specified | Required |
| Audit logging | General | Automated |
| Workforce access termination notice | Not specified | Within 24 hours |

---

### Status

The NPRM was published January 6, 2025, with public comments due by March 7, 2025. Over 2,800 comments were received. The final rule is expected in **May 2026**, with enforcement likely beginning in **2027** after a transition period. These proposals are **not yet final** — the current 2013-era Security Rule remains in force.

**Sources:** HHS OCR NPRM Fact Sheet (hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/hipaa-security-rule-nprm/factsheet), Federal Register Notice (federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/06/2024-30983), DLA Piper analysis (dlapiper.com), Morgan Lewis analysis (morganlewis.com), Maynard Nexsen analysis (maynardnexsen.com), Paul Hastings analysis (paulhastings.com).

---

## Substantive Differences in Trustworthiness Characteristics: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023) vs. 2022 Working Drafts

The evolution of trustworthiness characteristics across the NIST AI RMF drafts represents one of the most significant structural and conceptual shifts in the framework. There were **two 2022 drafts** — the **Initial Draft (March 2022)** and the **Second Draft (August 2022)** — and the changes between them and the final **AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023)** are substantial.

---

### 1. First Draft (March 2022): A Three-Class Taxonomy

The initial draft organized trustworthiness characteristics into a **hierarchical, three-class taxonomy** (NIST Initial Draft, §5):

| Category | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| **Technical Characteristics** | Accuracy, Reliability, Robustness, Resilience/ML Security |
| **Socio-Technical Characteristics** | Explainability, Interpretability, Privacy, Safety, Managing Bias |
| **Guiding Principles** | Fairness, Accountability, Transparency |

This taxonomy implied a **separation between "hard" technical metrics** (under direct control of designers/developers, measurable via statistical methods) and **"soft" socio-technical factors** (requiring human judgment, relating to societal perception), with guiding principles sitting above as overarching norms. It also treated certain characteristics as distinct that would later be merged (e.g., Accuracy and Reliability were separate; Robustness and Resilience/Security were separate from each other).

---

### 2. Second Draft (August 2022): The Flat, Interrelated List

The Second Draft made a **decisive break** from the three-class taxonomy. As noted by commentators at the time, this was "one of the most significant changes" (DWT, August 2022). The Second Draft collapsed the hierarchy into a **flat list of seven interrelated characteristics**, none elevated above the others:

1. **Valid and Reliable** (merging Accuracy + Reliability + Robustness)
2. **Safe** (elevated from a sub-characteristic to a standalone)
3. **Secure and Resilient** (merged from Resilience/ML Security)
4. **Accountable and Transparent** (merged from two Guiding Principles)
5. **Explainable and Interpretable** (retained as paired)
6. **Privacy-Enhanced** (retained, renamed from "Privacy")
7. **Fair — with Harmful Bias Managed** (merged Fairness + Managing Bias)

The Second Draft explicitly stated that all seven are **interrelated** and that tradeoffs among them must be balanced — a conceptual shift away from the first draft's implication that technical characteristics were foundational and guiding principles were aspirational.

---

### 3. AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023): Structural Refinement & Visual Hierarchy

The final version **retained the same seven characteristics** from the Second Draft but introduced two critical refinements:

#### (a) Figure 4 — A Nuanced Visual Hierarchy

While the Second Draft said none of the seven were "elevated above others," the final 1.0 introduced **Figure 4**, which gives the characteristics a **structured spatial relationship** (NIST AI 100-1, §3):

- **Valid & Reliable** is positioned as the **base** — described as "a necessary condition of trustworthiness" upon which the other characteristics rest.
- **Accountable & Transparent** is shown as a **vertical box spanning all other characteristics**, because it "relates to all other characteristics."
- The remaining five (Safe, Secure & Resilient, Explainable & Interpretable, Privacy-Enhanced, Fair) sit between them.

This is a substantive refinement: it acknowledges that while all characteristics must be balanced, **validity and reliability are prerequisites** — you cannot have a trustworthy system that is inaccurate or unreliable — and **accountability and transparency are cross-cutting enablers** for all others.

#### (b) Deeper Definitions and ISO Anchoring

The final version grounded definitions in formal standards more explicitly than the drafts:

- **Validation**: anchored to ISO 9000:2015 ("confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled")
- **Reliability**: anchored to ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022 ("ability of an item to perform as required, without failure, for a given time interval, under given conditions")
- **Information integrity**: added as a concept derived from the 2022 White House Roadmap for Researchers on Priorities Related to Information Integrity Research and Development

#### (c) Explicit Tradeoff Language

The final version sharpened the tradeoff discussion, adding language not present in the Second Draft: "Highly secure but unfair systems, accurate but opaque and uninterpretable systems, and inaccurate but secure, privacy-enhanced, and transparent systems are all undesirable" (NIST AI 100-1, §3). This concrete framing of undesirable combinations was new.

---

### Summary Table

| Aspect | First Draft (Mar 2022) | Second Draft (Aug 2022) | Final 1.0 (Jan 2023) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Structure** | 3-class taxonomy (Technical / Socio-Technical / Guiding Principles) | Flat list of 7 interrelated characteristics | 7 characteristics with Figure 4 spatial hierarchy |
| **Accuracy & Reliability** | Separate characteristics | Merged into "Valid and Reliable" | Retained as merged; designated as "necessary condition" base |
| **Safety** | Sub-characteristic under Socio-Technical | Standalone characteristic | Retained as standalone |
| **Accountability & Transparency** | Separate Guiding Principles | Merged into one characteristic | Retained as merged; designated as cross-cutting vertical |
| **Fairness & Bias** | Separate (Fairness as Guiding Principle; Managing Bias as Socio-Technical) | Merged into "Fair — with Harmful Bias Managed" | Retained as merged |
| **ISO anchoring** | Minimal | Partial | Explicit (ISO 9000:2015, ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022) |
| **Tradeoff framing** | Implicit | Explicit but general | Explicit with concrete undesirable-combination examples |

The core substantive difference is therefore twofold: (1) the **abolition of the three-class taxonomy** in favor of a unified, non-hierarchical (but spatially structured) set of seven characteristics, and (2) the **elevation of "Valid & Reliable" as the necessary foundation** and "Accountable & Transparent" as the cross-cutting dimension in the final 1.0 — a nuance that the Second Draft's "none elevated above others" framing had not captured.

## What Changed: GPAI / Foundation Model Obligations — 2021 Commission Proposal vs. Final 2024 EU AI Act

### 1. The 2021 Commission Proposal: Complete Silence on Foundation Models

The European Commission's original April 2021 proposal contained **no provisions whatsoever** addressing general-purpose AI (GPAI) or foundation models. The proposal was structured entirely around a risk-based framework for *AI systems* — classifying them as prohibited, high-risk, or subject to transparency obligations (Title IV, Article 52). The concept of regulating the underlying *models* themselves (as distinct from the systems built on them) was absent. As the retrieval results confirm, the 2021 text focused on high-risk AI system requirements (data quality, technical documentation, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity) and transparency for chatbots and deep fakes — but nothing targeting foundation model providers.

### 2. The Parliament's June 2023 Amendments: Article 28b Introduced

The European Parliament, responding to the emergence of ChatGPT and other generative AI systems after 2022, adopted amendments on 14 June 2023 that introduced **Article 28b — "Obligations of the provider of a foundation model."** This was the first legislative text to impose direct duties on foundation model developers. Key obligations included:

- **Risk mitigation**: demonstrating through design, testing, and analysis the identification, reduction, and mitigation of reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, fundamental rights, the environment, democracy, and the rule of law (Art. 28b(2)(a)).
- **Data governance**: examining the suitability of data sources and possible biases (Art. 28b(2)(b)).
- **Performance & safety**: ensuring "appropriate levels" of performance, predictability, safety, and cybersecurity (Art. 28b(2)(c)).
- **Sustainability standards**: conforming to a range of environmental sustainability requirements (Art. 28b(2)(d)).
- **EU database registration**: registering the foundation model in an EU-wide database before making it available (Art. 28b(2)(f)).
- **Quality management system**: establishing a quality management system (Art. 28b(2)(g)).
- **Technical documentation**: maintaining technical documentation for 10 years (Art. 28b(3)).
- **Generative AI transparency**: additional obligations for generative AI systems (Art. 28b(4)).

This was a **single-tier, comprehensive regime** — all foundation model providers faced the same extensive obligations, closely mirroring many high-risk AI system requirements.

### 3. The Final 2024 Text (Chapter V, Articles 51–56): A Relaxed, Two-Tier Approach

Following contentious trilogue negotiations (Commission–Parliament–Council) in the second half of 2023, the final text adopted a significantly different architecture. The key changes:

#### (a) Terminology Shift
- "Foundation model" → **"general-purpose AI model"** (GPAI model), defined at Article 3(63) as an AI model "that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks."

#### (b) Two-Tier Structure (Articles 53 & 55)
The final Act splits obligations into two tiers:

**Tier 1 — All GPAI model providers (Article 53):**
- Draw up and keep up-to-date **technical documentation** (training/testing process, evaluation results) per Annex XI — provided to the AI Office and national authorities *upon request* (not proactively published).
- Draw up and make available **information and documentation to downstream providers** (those integrating the model into AI systems) per Annex XII, enabling them to understand capabilities and limitations.
- Put in place a **copyright policy** to comply with EU copyright law, including respecting opt-outs under Article 4(3) of the DSM Directive (2019/790).
- Draw up and **publicly disclose** a sufficiently detailed summary of training data content.

**Tier 2 — GPAI models with systemic risk (Article 55):**
- **Perform model evaluation**, including adversarial testing.
- **Assess and mitigate systemic risks** at Union level.
- **Track, document, and report serious incidents** to the AI Office and national authorities.
- Ensure **adequate cybersecurity protections**.

#### (c) What Was Removed / Relaxed vs. the Parliament Proposal

| Parliament Proposal (Art. 28b) | Final 2024 Act (Chapter V) |
|---|---|
| Mandatory **quality management system** | **Removed** |
| Mandatory **registration in EU database** before market placement | **Removed** |
| **Data governance** obligations (examining data suitability, biases) | **Removed** (replaced by lighter training data summary) |
| **Sustainability / environmental standards** | **Removed** |
| **Performance, predictability, safety** as standalone obligations | **Removed** (folded into systemic-risk tier only) |
| **10-year documentation retention** mandate | **Removed** |
| Single-tier: all foundation models treated equally | **Two-tier**: lighter obligations for most; heavier only for systemic-risk models |
| Public-facing disclosure emphasis | Only **one** public-facing disclosure (training data summary) |

#### (d) Systemic Risk Classification (Article 51)
The final Act defines systemic risk through a **presumptive compute threshold** (training above 10²⁵ FLOPS) plus Commission discretion based on Annex XIII criteria (number of parameters, dataset size, input/output modalities, benchmarks, reach, etc.). The Parliament's approach was less clearly delineated.

#### (e) Open-Source Exception (Article 53(2))
The final Act includes a **carve-out** for free and open-source models (where parameters, weights, architecture, and usage information are publicly available) from the Article 53(1)(a)–(b) documentation obligations. This exception **does not apply** to systemic-risk models. The Parliament proposal had no comparable open-source exemption.

#### (f) Codes of Practice (Article 56) and Centralised Enforcement
The final Act relies heavily on **codes of practice** (elaborated by the AI Office with multi-stakeholder input) as the primary compliance mechanism, with harmonised standards to follow. The AI Office has **exclusive competence** for supervising GPAI model obligations — a centralised enforcement model not present in the 2021 proposal (which relied on Member State-level market surveillance).

### 4. Summary of the Trajectory

| Stage | GPAI / Foundation Model Provisions |
|---|---|
| **2021 Commission Proposal** | **None.** Silent on foundation models entirely. |
| **June 2023 Parliament Amendments** | **Article 28b:** Comprehensive, single-tier obligations (risk mitigation, data governance, performance, sustainability, QMS, database registration, 10-year documentation). |
| **Final 2024 Act** | **Chapter V (Articles 51–56):** Relaxed, two-tier approach. Tier 1: technical documentation (on request), downstream info, copyright policy, training data summary. Tier 2 (systemic risk only): model evaluation, adversarial testing, risk mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity. Open-source exception. Codes of practice as primary compliance pathway. |

The shift from the Parliament's more fundamental-rights-focused, comprehensive approach to the final text reflects the influence of Member States (in the Council) and industry lobbying during trilogue, resulting in a framework that the policy literature describes as "somewhat relaxed" and more "industry-friendly" — focusing primarily on transparency and information-sharing for most GPAI models, with heavier obligations reserved for the most capable (systemic-risk) models only.

## Article 4: AI Literacy

Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in, and considering the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used.

**Article 9: Risk Management System**
### Article 9: Risk Management System

1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps:

(a) the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose;

(b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse;

(c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72;

(d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

3. The risks referred to in this Article shall concern only those which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information.

4. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall give due consideration to the effects and possible interaction resulting from the combined application of the requirements set out in this Section, with a view to minimising risks more effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures to fulfil those requirements.

5. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall be such that the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable. In identifying the most appropriate risk management measures, the following shall be ensured:

(a) elimination or reduction of risks identified and evaluated pursuant to paragraph 2 in as far as technically feasible through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system;

(b) where appropriate, implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that cannot be eliminated;

(c) provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

**Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity**
### Article 15: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.

2. To address the technical aspects of how to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness set out in paragraph 1 and any other relevant performance metrics, the Commission shall, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, encourage, as appropriate, the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies.

3. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.

4. High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems. Technical and organisational measures shall be taken in this regard.

The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.

High-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service shall be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations (feedback loops), and as to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures.

5. High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions aiming to ensure the cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems shall be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks.

The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.

## Key Differences: 1995 EU Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC) vs. GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)

The GDPR did not merely update the 1995 Directive — it fundamentally transformed the EU data protection landscape. Below are the most significant differences for organisations processing personal data.

---

### 1. Legal Form: Directive → Regulation

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| A **Directive** requiring transposition into national law by each Member State, resulting in a patchwork of 28 different national implementations. | A **Regulation** directly applicable in all Member States without national transposition, creating a single, harmonised legal framework across the EU (Article 1, GDPR). |

**Impact for organisations:** One set of rules across the EU, reducing legal fragmentation and compliance costs for cross-border operations.

---

### 2. Territorial Scope — Dramatic Expansion

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Applied primarily to controllers established in the EU or using equipment in the EU for processing. | **Article 3 GDPR** extends to any organisation anywhere in the world that (a) offers goods or services to individuals in the EU, or (b) monitors the behaviour of individuals in the EU. Non-EU controllers/processors must also designate an **EU Representative** (Article 27). |

**Impact:** Even organisations with no physical EU presence are now directly subject to EU data protection law.

---

### 3. Consent — Far Stricter Standard

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Consent could be implied or inferred from circumstances; "opt-out" models were common. | **Article 4(11)** defines consent as a "freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication" requiring a "clear affirmative action." **Article 7** requires controllers to *demonstrate* consent was obtained, mandates that withdrawal be "as easy as to give," and prohibits bundling consent as a condition of service where unnecessary. **Article 8** introduces specific protections for children's consent (age 16, with Member State option down to 13). |

**Impact:** Pre-ticked boxes, silence, and inactivity no longer constitute valid consent. Organisations must redesign consent mechanisms and maintain auditable consent records.

---

### 4. New and Enhanced Data Subject Rights

| Right | 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|---|
| **Access** (Art. 15) | Basic right of access existed. | Expanded: must now include retention periods, right to lodge complaints, information about safeguards for international transfers, and the right to a copy in a commonly used electronic format. |
| **Erasure / "Right to be Forgotten"** (Art. 17) | Not explicitly codified. | A fully articulated right: data must be erased where no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing was unlawful. If data has been made public, the controller must take "reasonable steps" to inform other controllers of the erasure request. |
| **Data Portability** (Art. 20) | **Did not exist.** | Entirely new: data subjects can receive their data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and have it transmitted directly to another controller where technically feasible. |
| **Automated Decision-Making** (Art. 22) | Limited protections. | Strengthened: explicit right not to be subject to solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects, with mandatory safeguards including human intervention. |

---

### 5. Accountability — From Passive Compliance to Active Demonstration

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Required compliance with data protection principles but did not mandate proactive documentation. | **Article 5(2)** introduces the **accountability principle**: controllers must not only comply but *demonstrate* compliance. This is operationalised through: |

Key new accountability obligations under GDPR:

- **Records of Processing Activities (Art. 30):** Controllers and processors must maintain detailed written records of all processing activities (a new, affirmative documentation duty).
- **Data Protection Impact Assessments — DPIAs (Art. 35):** Mandatory for high-risk processing (e.g., large-scale profiling, systematic monitoring, special category data).
- **Prior Consultation (Art. 36):** Where a DPIA indicates high residual risk, the controller must consult the supervisory authority *before* processing.
- **Data Protection by Design and by Default (Art. 25):** Organisations must embed data protection into the design of systems and processes from the outset, not as an afterthought.
- **Data Protection Officer — DPO (Arts. 37–39):** Mandatory appointment for public authorities, organisations whose core activities involve large-scale systematic monitoring, or large-scale processing of special category data. The DPO must be independent, report to the highest management level, and cannot be penalised for performing their duties.

---

### 6. Breach Notification — Entirely New Obligation

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| **No breach notification requirement.** | **Articles 33–34** introduce mandatory breach notification: |
| | • To the supervisory authority: within **72 hours** of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk to individuals. |
| | • To affected data subjects: "without undue delay" where the breach is likely to result in **high risk** to their rights and freedoms. |
| | • Processors must notify controllers "without undue delay." |

**Impact:** Organisations need incident response plans, breach detection capabilities, and clear internal escalation procedures.

---

### 7. Direct Processor Liability

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Processors were primarily regulated through contracts with controllers; enforcement was directed at controllers. | **Article 28** imposes direct statutory obligations on processors (e.g., security measures, record-keeping, breach notification, DPO appointment, restrictions on sub-processors). Processors face **direct fines and liability** (Art. 82–83). |

---

### 8. Fines and Enforcement — Transformative Increase

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Fines were set at national level, generally modest, and varied widely between Member States. No harmonised enforcement mechanism. | **Article 83** introduces two tiers of administrative fines: |
| | • **Up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover** (whichever is higher) for infringements relating to record-keeping, DPO, DPIA, security, breach notification, etc. |
| | • **Up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover** (whichever is higher) for infringements of core principles, consent conditions, data subject rights, and international transfer rules. |

**Impact:** Fines are now potentially existential for large organisations and serve as a genuine deterrent.

---

### 9. One-Stop Shop and Consistency Mechanism

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| No formal cross-border coordination mechanism; organisations dealt with multiple national DPAs independently. | **Articles 56 and 60–63** establish the **one-stop shop**: organisations with cross-border processing deal primarily with a single **Lead Supervisory Authority** (in the Member State of their main establishment). The **consistency mechanism** ensures cooperation among DPAs and uniform interpretation via the European Data Protection Board (EDPB). |

---

### 10. International Data Transfers — More Mechanisms, Stricter Safeguards

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Adequacy decisions and standard contractual clauses existed but were limited. | GDPR expands transfer tools: **Binding Corporate Rules** (Art. 47) are now explicitly codified; **codes of conduct** (Art. 40) and **certification mechanisms** (Art. 42) can serve as transfer safeguards; **Article 48** restricts enforcement of third-country judgments. Existing adequacy decisions under the Directive remain valid until replaced (Art. 45(9)). |

---

### 11. Codes of Conduct and Certification

| 1995 Directive | GDPR |
|---|---|
| Not provided for. | **Articles 40–43** encourage sector-specific codes of conduct and data protection certification mechanisms, seals, and marks — including a "European Data Protection Seal" — to help organisations demonstrate compliance. |

---

### Summary Table

| Dimension | Directive 95/46/EC | GDPR |
|---|---|---|
| **Legal form** | Directive (national transposition) | Regulation (directly applicable) |
| **Territorial reach** | EU establishment / equipment | Global — targeting or monitoring EU persons |
| **Consent standard** | Could be implied | Unambiguous, affirmative, demonstrable |
| **Accountability** | Passive compliance | Active demonstration (Art. 5(2)) |
| **DPO** | Not required | Mandatory for many organisations |
| **DPIA** | Not required | Mandatory for high-risk processing |
| **Breach notification** | None | 72 hours to DPA; notify data subjects |
| **Right to erasure** | Limited | Codified "right to be forgotten" |
| **Data portability** | None | New right (Art. 20) |
| **Processor liability** | Indirect (via controller) | Direct statutory obligations and fines |
| **Fines** | Modest, nationally variable | Up to €20M / 4% global turnover |
| **Cross-border enforcement** | Fragmented | One-stop shop + consistency mechanism |
| **Certification / codes** | None | Encouraged (Arts. 40–43) |

For organisations, the shift from the 1995 Directive to the GDPR represents a move from a fragmented, relatively light-touch compliance environment to a unified, high-stakes regulatory regime where accountability, transparency, and demonstrable compliance are central obligations.

## Summary: The 2022 SOC 2 "Points of Focus" Update

The 2022 update to the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria **did not change the certifiable criteria themselves — it only revised the guidance (the "Points of Focus")**. The underlying 2017 Trust Services Criteria (codified in TSP Section 100) remain unchanged and continue to serve as the suitable criteria for evaluating controls in any SOC 2 engagement.

### What the AICPA itself states

The AICPA is explicit on this point:

> *"The changes to the points of focus in the 2022 revisions do not, in any way, alter the criteria in the 2017 TSC. Such criteria continue to be suitable criteria for use when evaluating controls in any trust services engagement."* (TSP Section 100, 2017 Trust Services Criteria with Revised Points of Focus — 2022)

### What actually changed

The revisions were limited to the **Points of Focus** — the illustrative characteristics that help management and practitioners evaluate whether controls are suitably designed and operating effectively. The updates were intended to:

1. **Address evolving technologies, threats, and vulnerabilities** — reflecting the changing risk landscape.
2. **Address changing legal/regulatory requirements and cultural expectations regarding privacy** — including clearer differentiation between points of focus applicable to data controllers vs. data processors.
3. **Address data management topics** — such as data storage, backup, and retention, particularly in relation to confidentiality.
4. **Provide additional clarity on disclosure requirements** — including guidance on how controls meet the requirements of a process or control framework, and disclosure of risk assessment processes.

### Practical significance

- **No new criteria were added; no existing criteria were removed or substantively altered.** The 17 COSO-aligned principles and the supplemental criteria (logical and physical access controls, system operations, change management, and monitoring) remain exactly as they were in 2017.
- Points of focus are explicitly **not mandatory** — the TSC states that "use of the trust services criteria does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed" and that management may customize or identify additional points of focus based on the entity's specific circumstances.
- For organizations undergoing a SOC 2 examination, the 2022 update means practitioners will likely consider these refreshed points of focus when evaluating control design and effectiveness, but the bar for certification — the criteria themselves — has not moved.

### Bottom line

The 2022 update was a **guidance-only refresh**. It modernised the illustrative points of focus to keep pace with technology, privacy, and data management developments, but the certifiable Trust Services Criteria remain the 2017 criteria, unchanged.

question.question: How has SR 11-7 guidance on ongoing model monitoring evolved between the 2011 original and the 2026 SR 26-2 revision, particularly for AI/ML models?

SR 26-2 (2026) explicitly extends monitoring to AI/ML: continuous monitoring of distributional drift, performance decay, fairness/bias metrics, and emergent behaviour; explicit treatment of self-learning systems with retraining controls; vendor-AI-model monitoring obligations; and tighter governance over model changes via continuous-deployment pipelines. The 2026 revision treats the model lifecycle as continuous rather than periodic.

## Evolution of Ongoing Model Monitoring: SR 11-7 (2011) → SR 26-2 (2026)

The evolution of ongoing model monitoring from SR 11-7 to SR 26-2 represents one of the most significant shifts in U.S. banking model risk management in over a decade. Below is a structured analysis of the key changes, with particular attention to AI/ML implications.

---

### 1. Structural Elevation: From Sub-Component to Co-Equal Pillar

**SR 11-7 (2011):** Ongoing monitoring was treated as one element within the broader "Model Validation" framework (Section V). It was one of three validation components — conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis — but in practice, monitoring was often the least resourced of the three.

**SR 26-2 (2026):** The agencies renamed Section V from **"Model Validation"** to **"Model Validation (and Monitoring)"** — a deliberate structural signal that elevates ongoing monitoring to a co-equal status alongside validation itself. This is not merely cosmetic; it reflects the supervisory view that for modern, dynamic models (especially AI/ML), point-in-time validation is insufficient without robust continuous monitoring.

> *Source: Quant StackExchange analysis of SR 26-2 vs SR 11-7; ValidMind SR 26-2 overview.*

---

### 2. From Prescriptive Annual Cycles to Risk-Based, Trigger-Driven Cadence

**SR 11-7:** The original guidance was widely interpreted as establishing a default annual revalidation cycle for all models, regardless of materiality. Monitoring frequency was largely calendar-driven. The guidance was detailed and prescriptive about specific statistical tests, VaR back-testing procedures, and organizational separation requirements.

**SR 26-2:** Monitoring frequency is **no longer fixed**. It is explicitly tied to three factors:

- **Model materiality** (a function of model exposure × purpose)
- **Change velocity** (how quickly the model's environment, data, or methodology shifts)
- **Data availability** (whether performance data is sufficient for meaningful assessment)

Critically, SR 26-2 allows **immaterial models to operate on a trigger-only basis** — monitoring activates when conditions change, not on a fixed calendar. Material models may warrant more frequent or even continuous review.

> *Source: Domino.ai SR 26-2 dictionary; ValidMind comparison table.*

---

### 3. Shift in Weight: From Validation-Heavy to Monitoring-Heavy

**SR 11-7:** The operational gravity of MRM programs centered on periodic, point-in-time full revalidations. Monitoring was often a lighter-weight activity between validation cycles.

**SR 26-2:** The guidance explicitly **shifts weight from validation to ongoing monitoring**, particularly for:

- **Lower-materiality models** — where full revalidation may be disproportionate
- **Frequently updated models** — where static validation cannot keep pace with change cycles
- **Vendor/third-party models** — where the bank lacks full visibility into development but can monitor outcomes

The goal is not to replicate full validation for every model change but to **maintain confidence in performance and detect drift quickly**.

> *Source: ValidMind "SR 26-2: What Every Bank Needs to Know"; Ankura validation analysis.*

---

### 4. AI/ML-Specific Monitoring Provisions

This is where the evolution is most pronounced:

| Dimension | SR 11-7 (2011) | SR 26-2 (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Drift detection** | Implicit; back-testing focused | Explicit requirement for **concept drift and data drift** detection |
| **Automation** | Not addressed | Automated monitoring systems with **real-time drift alerts** expected |
| **Re-triggering** | Calendar-based revalidation | Automated triggers for re-validation when drift thresholds breached |
| **Model inventory** | Static inventory | **Dynamic inventory** — systems must auto-flag models for re-review when market conditions or data relevance change |
| **Explainability** | Not explicitly addressed | Implicit in governance and documentation expectations; BIS and agency guidance increasingly emphasizes explainability for AI/ML |
| **Fairness/bias** | Not addressed | Emerging expectation; KPMG and BIS guidance tie fairness monitoring to MRM frameworks |
| **GenAI/Agentic AI** | Not contemplated | Explicitly noted as out of scope but agencies state that **core MRM principles still apply** |

> *Source: Lumenova AI SR 26-2 actionable guide; Domino.ai; BIS FSI Papers No. 24 on explainability; KPMG AI/ML MRM framework.*

---

### 5. From Prescriptive Rules to Principles-Based Flexibility

**SR 11-7:** ~20 pages of dense, prescriptive expectations. Enforced as de facto binding — deviations routinely triggered Matters Requiring Attention (MRAs).

**SR 26-2:** Roughly half the length. The introductory letter explicitly states the guidance **does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements**, and non-compliance alone will not result in supervisory criticism. This principles-based approach gives institutions flexibility but shifts the burden to **articulate and defend their monitoring choices** without relying on detailed regulatory prescriptions.

> *Source: Domino.ai "What changes with SR 26-2"; PwC "Our Take" April 24, 2026.*

---

### 6. Practical Implications for AI/ML Models

For AI/ML models specifically, the evolution means:

1. **Continuous monitoring is no longer optional.** The dynamic, non-stationary nature of ML models (susceptible to concept drift, data drift, and emergent behaviors) makes annual validation cycles inadequate. SR 26-2 effectively mandates that monitoring cadence match model velocity.

2. **Automated infrastructure is expected.** Banks need systems that can track performance metrics in near-real-time, compare predictions to actuals, detect distributional shifts in inputs and outputs, and trigger alerts — all without manual intervention.

3. **Monitoring must be linked to business conditions.** SR 26-2 ties monitoring explicitly to changes in products, portfolios, data relevance, and market/economic conditions — all of which can degrade AI/ML model performance between formal reviews.

4. **Documentation burden shifts.** Rather than documenting exhaustive validation tests, institutions must now document their **monitoring rationale**: why a given cadence is appropriate, what thresholds trigger re-review, and how monitoring findings feed back into model governance.

5. **Explainability and fairness are emerging expectations.** While not codified as explicit SR 26-2 requirements, the broader regulatory ecosystem (BIS, interagency statements) increasingly expects AI/ML models to be monitored for explainability degradation and fairness drift alongside predictive performance.

> *Sources: Lumenova AI; ValidMind; Ankura; BIS FSI Papers; KPMG.*

---

### Summary

The evolution from SR 11-7 to SR 26-2 transforms ongoing monitoring from a **calendar-driven, validation-adjacent activity** into a **risk-based, continuous, and co-equal pillar** of model risk management. For AI/ML models, this is not merely an incremental change — it represents a fundamental reorientation toward the reality that modern models degrade continuously, not annually, and that monitoring infrastructure must be automated, dynamic, and tightly coupled to governance.

## How the HITECH Act of 2009 Transformed HIPAA's Breach-Notification Regime

### 1. Pre-HITECH (2003 HIPAA): No Federal Breach Notification Requirement

Under the original HIPAA Privacy Rule (effective April 2003) and Security Rule (effective April 2005), **there was no federal breach-notification obligation whatsoever**. The 2003 framework focused on setting standards for permissible uses and disclosures of PHI and requiring administrative, physical, and technical safeguards — but it was silent on what a covered entity had to do when a breach occurred.

In practice, breach notification was governed by a **patchwork of state laws**, most notably California's pioneering data breach notification law (SB 1386, 2003). There was no requirement to notify HHS, no federal timeline, and no obligation to notify the media. A covered entity could experience a breach and, under federal HIPAA alone, have no duty to inform affected individuals.

### 2. The HITECH Act (2009): A Comprehensive Federal Breach-Notification Framework

Enacted as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA), the HITECH Act's **Section 13402** created an entirely new breach-notification regime, codified at **45 CFR §§ 164.400–164.414** (Subpart D). The key changes:

| Dimension | Pre-HITECH (2003) | Post-HITECH (2009+) |
|---|---|---|
| **Federal notification duty** | None | Mandatory for breaches of *unsecured* PHI |
| **Notice to individuals** | Not required | Required without unreasonable delay, ≤ 60 days (§ 164.404) |
| **Notice to HHS** | Not required | Required; contemporaneous if ≥ 500 individuals; annually if < 500 (§ 164.408) |
| **Notice to media** | Not required | Required if breach involves > 500 residents of a State (§ 164.406) |
| **Business associates** | No direct notification duty | Must notify covered entity within 60 days (§ 164.410) |
| **Enforcement / penalties** | Limited; no breach-specific penalties | Tiered civil money penalties up to $1.5M/year; state AG enforcement authority |
| **"Harm threshold" (2009 IFR)** | N/A | Notification required only if breach posed "significant risk of financial, reputational, or other harm" |
| **Risk-assessment standard (2013 Omnibus Rule)** | N/A | Presumption of breach; notification required unless entity demonstrates "low probability that PHI has been compromised" via a 4-factor risk assessment (§ 164.402) |

### 3. The "Unsecured PHI" Safe Harbor

The HITECH Act introduced the concept of **"unsecured protected health information"** (§ 164.402). If PHI is rendered unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable through technologies specified by the Secretary (i.e., encryption or destruction per NIST standards), a breach of that data does **not** trigger notification obligations. This safe harbor did not exist in the 2003 framework because there was no notification duty to trigger in the first place.

### 4. The Harm Threshold → Risk Assessment Evolution

A critical nuance: the **2009 Interim Final Rule** (published August 24, 2009) adopted a **"risk of harm"** standard — covered entities needed to notify only if the breach posed a *significant risk of financial, reputational, or other harm* to the individual. This was widely criticized as too subjective and inconsistent with Congressional intent.

The **2013 Omnibus Final Rule** (effective March 26, 2013; compliance by September 23, 2013) replaced this with a **presumption-of-breach** standard. Now, any impermissible acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of PHI is *presumed* to be a notifiable breach unless the covered entity or business associate demonstrates — through a documented, four-factor risk assessment — that there is a **low probability the PHI has been compromised** (§ 164.402(2)). The four factors are:

1. Nature and extent of PHI involved (including likelihood of re-identification)
2. The unauthorized person who used the PHI or to whom it was disclosed
3. Whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed
4. The extent to which the risk has been mitigated

This shifted the burden: under the 2009 IFR, the entity had to prove *harm was likely* to trigger notification; under the 2013 rule, the entity must prove *compromise is unlikely* to avoid notification.

### 5. Business Associate Direct Liability

The 2003 HIPAA rules applied directly only to covered entities. Business associates were bound only through contractual chain (business associate agreements). HITECH made business associates **directly liable** for breach notification: they must notify the covered entity of a breach without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days from discovery (§ 164.410). The 2013 Omnibus Rule extended this further by making business associates directly subject to the full Breach Notification Rule.

### 6. HHS Wall of Shame

HITECH also mandated that HHS publicly post breaches involving 500 or more individuals on its website — the so-called **"Wall of Shame"** — which has become a significant reputational enforcement mechanism with no pre-HITECH equivalent.

---

### Summary

The HITECH Act did not merely *amend* HIPAA's breach-notification regime — it **created it from scratch**. The 2003 HIPAA framework had no federal breach-notification requirement at all. HITECH introduced a multi-layered notification system (individuals, HHS, media), a 60-day clock, the unsecured-PHI safe harbor, business associate duties, and — after the 2013 Omnibus Rule refinement — a presumption-of-breach standard backed by a four-factor risk assessment. What began as a regulatory gap filled only by state law became one of the most consequential federal data-breach notification regimes in the United States.
