## Chapter III: Rights of the Data Subject

**Article 4 — Definitions**
### Article 4 — Definitions

For the purposes of this Regulation:

‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person;

‘processing’ means any operation or set of operations which is performed on personal data or on sets of personal data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation or alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, alignment or combination, restriction, erasure or destruction;

‘restriction of processing’ means the marking of stored personal data with the aim of limiting their processing in the future;

‘profiling’ means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person’s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements;

‘pseudonymisation’ means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person;

‘filing system’ means any structured set of personal data which are accessible according to specific criteria, whether centralised, decentralised or dispersed on a functional or geographical basis;

‘processor’ means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which processes personal data on behalf of the controller;

**Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default**
### Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default

Taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risks of varying likelihood and severity for rights and freedoms of natural persons posed by the processing, the controller shall, both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself, implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, which are designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing in order to meet the requirements of this Regulation and protect the rights of data subjects.

1The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. 2That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility. 3In particular, such measures shall ensure that by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual’s intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons.

### Article 5 — Principles relating to processing of personal data

processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’);

adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’);

processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (‘integrity and confidentiality’).

**Article 1 — Subject-matter and objectives**
### Article 1 — Subject-matter and objectives

This Regulation lays down rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the free movement of personal data.

This Regulation protects fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons and in particular their right to the protection of personal data.

The free movement of personal data within the Union shall be neither restricted nor prohibited for reasons connected with the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data.

### Article 29 — Processing under the authority of the controller or processor

The processor and any person acting under the authority of the controller or of the processor, who has access to personal data, shall not process those data except on instructions from the controller, unless required to do so by Union or Member State law.

question.question: Compare SOC 2 CC7.4 (security incident response) with GDPR Article 33 (notification to supervisory authority) on incident-response obligations.
question.expected_answer: SOC 2 CC7.4 requires the entity to respond to identified security events by executing a defined incident-response programme to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents. Specific elements: incident-response plan, defined roles, communication procedures, root-cause analysis, and post-incident review. GDPR Article 33 imposes a specific external obligation: notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach (unless unlikely to result in risk to data subjects), including specified content (nature of breach, categories/numbers affected, contact, likely consequences, measures taken). SOC 2 covers internal handling; GDPR adds an external regulatory clock and content requirements specifically for *personal data* breaches.

## Comparison: SOC 2 CC7.4 vs. GDPR Article 33 — Incident-Response Obligations

### 1. Scope and Trigger

| Dimension | SOC 2 CC7.4 | GDPR Article 33 |
|-----------|-------------|-----------------|
| **Trigger event** | Any **security incident** — a system event that requires action to prevent or reduce impact on service commitments and system requirements (per the SOC 2 glossary definitions of "system incident" and "security incident") | A **personal data breach** — a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, personal data |
| **Scope of harm** | Broad: covers security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy across all five trust services categories | Narrower but deeper: focused exclusively on risks to the **rights and freedoms of natural persons** |
| **Risk threshold** | No explicit risk threshold — any identified security incident triggers the response program | Notification required **unless** the breach is "unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons" (Art. 33(1)) |

### 2. Core Obligation

**SOC 2 CC7.4** (full criterion text):
> "The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident-response program to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents, as appropriate."

The criterion is supported by 11 points of focus:
- **Assigns Roles and Responsibilities** — Designated personnel with defined incident-response duties
- **Contains Security Incidents** — Procedures to contain the scope and impact
- **Mitigates Ongoing Security Incidents** — Actions to reduce ongoing harm
- **Ends Threats Posed by Security Incidents** — Closure of vulnerabilities, removal of unauthorized access
- **Restores Operations** — Returning affected environments to functional operation
- **Develops and Implements Communication Protocols for Security Incidents** — Defined communication procedures
- **Obtains Understanding of Nature of Incident and Determines Containment Strategy**
- **Remediates Identified Vulnerabilities**
- **Communicates Remediation Activities**
- **Evaluates the Effectiveness of Incident Response**
- **Periodically Evaluates Incidents** — Reviews incident patterns and root causes for system improvement

Additional privacy-specific points of focus include:
- **Applies Breach Response Procedures** — for confirmed privacy incidents
- **Communicates Unauthorized Use and Disclosure** — to data subjects, legal/regulatory authorities, and others as required
- **Application of Sanctions** — evaluating and sanctioning individuals involved in unauthorized use/disclosure

**GDPR Article 33**:
- **Controller obligation**: Notify the supervisory authority **without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours** after becoming aware of the breach (Art. 33(1))
- **Processor obligation**: Notify the controller **without undue delay** after becoming aware (Art. 33(2))
- **Late notification**: Must be accompanied by **reasons for the delay** (Art. 33(1))
- **Content requirements** (Art. 33(3)):
  - Nature of the breach, including categories and approximate number of data subjects and records
  - Name and contact details of the DPO or contact point
  - Likely consequences of the breach
  - Measures taken or proposed to address the breach, including mitigation
- **Phased notification**: Information may be provided in phases if not all available at once (Art. 33(4))
- **Documentation**: Controller must **document** all breaches, including facts, effects, and remedial action, enabling supervisory authority verification (Art. 33(5))

### 3. External Notification Requirements

| Aspect | SOC 2 CC7.4 | GDPR Article 33 (+ Art. 34) |
|--------|-------------|-----------------------------|
| **Regulator notification** | Not explicitly mandated by CC7.4 itself; the privacy point of focus says communicate "to legal and regulatory authorities… as required" — i.e., defers to applicable law | **Mandatory** notification to supervisory authority within 72 hours (Art. 33) |
| **Data subject notification** | Privacy point of focus: communicate unauthorized use/disclosure to data subjects "as required" | **Mandatory** under Art. 34 when breach poses **high risk** to rights and freedoms; must be in "clear and plain language" |
| **Timing specificity** | No hard deadline specified in the criterion | **72-hour hard deadline** (with reasons for delay if missed) |
| **Prescribed content** | No prescribed notification content format | Detailed content requirements in Art. 33(3) and Art. 34(2) |

### 4. Lifecycle Coverage

SOC 2 CC7.4 covers the **full incident-response lifecycle**:
- Preparation (roles, communication protocols)
- Detection & analysis (understand nature, determine containment strategy)
- Containment, eradication & recovery (contain, mitigate, end threats, restore operations, remediate vulnerabilities)
- Post-incident activity (evaluate effectiveness, periodic review, lessons learned, improve procedures)

GDPR Article 33 is **narrower in lifecycle scope** — it focuses primarily on the **notification and documentation** phase. It does not prescribe containment, eradication, or recovery procedures (those fall under Art. 32 — security of processing). However, Art. 33(3)(d) does require describing "measures taken or proposed" to address the breach, which implicitly requires having such measures.

### 5. Penalties and Enforcement

| Framework | Penalty Structure |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **SOC 2** | No direct fines; non-compliance results in a qualified or adverse auditor opinion, which can have commercial consequences (loss of customers, contract termination). The DC4 description criteria require disclosure of incidents that resulted in fines, sanctions, or material effects. |
| **GDPR Art. 33** | Violations fall under **Art. 83(4)(a)** — the lower tier: up to **€10 million or 2% of global annual turnover**, whichever is higher. In practice, Art. 33 violations are often compounded with Art. 32 (security) violations, which can reach the higher tier of **€20 million or 4%**. GDPR enforcement in 2025 alone exceeded **€1.2 billion** in total fines. |

### 6. Key Gaps When Viewed Together

If an organization complies with SOC 2 CC7.4 but has not separately addressed GDPR:

1. **No 72-hour clock**: CC7.4 does not impose a specific notification deadline. An organization could have a "defined incident-response program" without meeting GDPR's strict 72-hour requirement.
2. **No prescribed notification content**: CC7.4's communication protocols are not required to include the specific data points Art. 33(3) mandates (categories of data subjects, approximate numbers, DPO contact, etc.).
3. **No mandatory breach documentation standard**: While CC7.4 requires periodic evaluation of incidents, it does not mandate the specific breach documentation that Art. 33(5) requires for supervisory authority verification.
4. **Risk threshold missing**: CC7.4 does not incorporate the GDPR's risk-to-natural-persons threshold for determining whether notification is required.
5. **Processor→Controller flow**: GDPR Art. 33(2) explicitly requires processors to notify controllers "without undue delay." CC7.4 does not address this upstream notification obligation in the data processing chain.

Conversely, GDPR Article 33 does not address what CC7.4 covers well:
- No requirement for defined roles and responsibilities
- No requirement for periodic evaluation of incident patterns
- No requirement for testing incident-recovery plans
- No requirement for evaluating incident response effectiveness

### 7. Summary

SOC 2 CC7.4 provides a **broad, process-oriented framework** for the full incident-response lifecycle across all trust services categories. GDPR Article 33 imposes a **narrower but legally binding, time-sensitive notification obligation** with specific content requirements and significant financial penalties. The two frameworks are complementary: CC7.4 builds the operational incident-response capability, while Art. 33 mandates the specific regulatory notification output. Organizations subject to both must ensure their CC7.4-aligned incident response program includes the 72-hour notification trigger, prescribed content, and documentation requirements of GDPR Art. 33.

question.question: How do EU AI Act Article 14 (human oversight) and SR 11-7's 'effective challenge' principle each ensure that automated/model decisions remain subject to human review?
question.expected_answer: EU AI Act Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed in a way that natural persons can effectively oversee them during the period in which the system is in use. Specific measures: appropriate human-machine interface tools, ability to interpret outputs, ability to override or refuse to use the system, ability to interrupt operation via a 'stop' button, awareness of automation bias, and competence/authority/training of oversight personnel. SR 11-7's effective challenge is an organisational principle: critical analysis of models by objective, informed parties — qualified people who are independent from development and whose review can effect change. EU AI Act is product-design focused (user-facing oversight controls); SR 11-7 is governance focused (organisational independence and authority).

output.answer:
I now have sufficient material to provide a thorough comparative analysis. Let me synthesize the findings.

---

## Comparative Analysis: EU AI Act Article 14 vs. SR 11-7 "Effective Challenge"

Both frameworks aim to ensure that automated/model-driven decisions do not operate in a human-free vacuum, but they approach this goal from fundamentally different regulatory philosophies — one is a **product-design mandate** and the other is a **governance-process mandate**.

---

### 1. EU AI Act Article 14 — Human Oversight as a Design Requirement

**Nature:** A binding, prescriptive regulation that applies to all high-risk AI systems placed on the EU market.

**Core mechanism:** Article 14 requires that human oversight be *built into the system itself* before it ever reaches the deployer. It operates at two levels:

#### A. Provider-level obligations (ex ante, design-phase)

Article 14(1) mandates that high-risk AI systems be "designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use."

Article 14(3) requires oversight measures to be ensured through one or both of:
- **(a)** Measures *built into the system* by the provider before market placement (technically feasible measures)
- **(b)** Measures *identified by the provider* and appropriate for implementation by the deployer

#### B. Deployer-level capabilities (operational-phase)

Article 14(4) enumerates five specific capabilities that the system must enable for human overseers:

| Capability | What it ensures |
|---|---|
| **(a)** Understand capacities and limitations; monitor for anomalies | Informed vigilance |
| **(b)** Remain aware of automation bias | Cognitive guardrail against over-reliance |
| **(c)** Correctly interpret outputs using available tools | Meaningful comprehension |
| **(d)** Decide not to use, or to disregard, override, or reverse outputs | **Decisional veto power** |
| **(e)** Intervene or interrupt via a "stop" button or similar safe-state procedure | **Operational kill-switch** |

#### C. The "two-person rule" (Article 14(5))

For certain Annex III systems (e.g., remote biometric identification), no action may be taken based on the AI's output unless *at least two natural persons* with competence, training, and authority have separately verified and confirmed the identification. This is a hard procedural safeguard — a double-human lock.

#### D. Deployer obligations (Article 26)

Article 26(2) reinforces Article 14 by requiring deployers to "assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support." This closes the loop: the provider builds the capability; the deployer must staff it properly.

---

### 2. SR 11-7 — "Effective Challenge" as a Governance Principle

**Nature:** Interagency supervisory guidance (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC), not a binding regulation. It applies to banking organizations' model risk management frameworks.

**Core mechanism:** Effective challenge is defined as:

> "the critical analysis conducted by **objective experts** who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring."

The guidance establishes **three essential pillars** for effective challenge:

#### A. Expertise
Individuals performing the challenge must have the **appropriate expertise** to conduct a critical and objective analysis. This means technical competence in the model's methodology, data, and domain — not merely general oversight skills.

#### B. Independence
The challengers must have **sufficient independence to maintain objectivity**. This is a structural requirement: the validation/oversight function must be separated from the model development function. SR 11-7 explicitly warns against "misalignment of incentives between different reporting lines, such as model development and validation groups."

#### C. Organizational Standing and Influence
Challengers must have the **organizational standing and influence to effect any change**. This is critical — it means effective challenge is not merely advisory. The challenger must have the institutional authority to compel remediation, reject a model, or require redevelopment.

#### D. Lifecycle-wide application

Unlike Article 14, which focuses on the operational use phase, effective challenge applies across the **entire model lifecycle**:
- **Development:** Challenge conceptual soundness, assumptions, data quality
- **Implementation:** Challenge the translation of model into production
- **Validation:** Independent review of performance, limitations, and ongoing fitness
- **Ongoing monitoring:** Challenge whether the model remains appropriate as conditions change

---

### 3. Key Structural Differences

| Dimension | EU AI Act Article 14 | SR 11-7 Effective Challenge |
|---|---|---|
| **Regulatory character** | Binding regulation with penalties (up to €15M or 3% of turnover) | Supervisory guidance (non-binding, but non-compliance may evidence unsafe practices) |
| **Primary duty-bearer** | Provider (design) + Deployer (operation) | Banking organization (governance framework) |
| **Timing focus** | Operational use (real-time oversight) | Entire model lifecycle (development through decommissioning) |
| **Human role** | Real-time overseer with veto/kill-switch powers | Independent expert reviewer with institutional authority |
| **Structural safeguard** | Human-machine interface design + two-person rule | Organizational separation (development vs. validation) |
| **Automation bias** | Explicitly addressed (Article 14(4)(b)) | Addressed implicitly through independence requirement |
| **Scope** | All high-risk AI systems in the EU market | Models used by U.S. banking organizations (focused on $30B+ assets) |

---

### 4. How They Complement Each Other

For a financial institution subject to both frameworks (e.g., a bank using high-risk AI in the EU), the two regimes create a **layered defense**:

- **Article 14** ensures that the *technical interface* allows a human to understand, question, and override the system at the moment of decision.
- **SR 11-7** ensures that *before and after* that moment, independent experts with real authority have critically examined whether the model is sound, whether its outputs are reliable, and whether it should continue to be used at all.

Article 14 is the **tactical, real-time safeguard**; SR 11-7 effective challenge is the **strategic, lifecycle governance safeguard**. One prevents a bad decision from going through unchecked; the other prevents a bad model from being relied upon in the first place.

---

### 5. Potential Gaps When Viewed Together

- **Article 14 does not mandate organizational independence** of the human overseer. A deployer could theoretically assign oversight to someone in the same reporting line that benefits from the AI's outputs — a gap that SR 11-7's independence pillar would catch.
- **SR 11-7 does not mandate real-time override capability.** It focuses on periodic validation and monitoring, not on-the-spot intervention. Article 14's "stop button" requirement fills this gap.
- **SR 11-7 (2026 edition) explicitly excludes generative AI and agentic AI** from its scope, while the EU AI Act covers these technologies. This creates a regulatory blind spot for U.S. banking organizations using generative AI models that would be classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act.

question.question: How does GDPR Article 22 (automated decision-making) interact with the EU AI Act's classification of certain AI systems as high-risk? Are there cases where Article 22 applies but the AI Act does not, or vice versa?
question.expected_answer: GDPR Article 22 applies to decisions based solely on automated processing — including profiling — that produce legal or similarly significant effects on a data subject. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI systems as high-risk based on Annex III categories (e.g. employment, creditworthiness, education) regardless of whether decisions are 'solely' automated. Overlap: automated credit scoring, automated hiring, automated benefit eligibility — both regimes typically apply. Article 22 applies but the AI Act may not: a fully-automated, legally-significant decision using a rules-engine that doesn't meet the AI Act's definition of an AI system (Article 3) or isn't in an Annex III use case. AI Act applies but Article 22 may not: an Annex III high-risk AI that supports rather than makes the decision, leaving a human in the loop (no longer 'solely automated' under Art 22). Both regimes can apply concurrently and create overlapping obligations (right to explanation, human review, fairness/bias controls).

## GDPR Article 22 vs. EU AI Act High-Risk Classification: Interaction, Overlap, and Gaps

### 1. The Two Frameworks at a Glance

**GDPR Article 22** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) establishes a **data subject right**: individuals have the right "not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her" (Art. 22(1)). It applies only when:

- The decision is **solely** automated (no meaningful human intervention);
- It produces **legal effects** or **similarly significant effects** on the data subject;
- **Personal data** is being processed (Art. 2 — material scope).

It has three exceptions: necessity for contract, explicit consent, or Union/Member State law authorization (Art. 22(2)), and imposes additional safeguards including the right to human intervention, to express one's point of view, and to contest the decision (Art. 22(3)).

**The EU AI Act** (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) takes a **product-safety and fundamental-rights approach**. It classifies AI systems as high-risk via two routes:

- **Article 6(1)**: The AI system is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in **Annex I** (e.g., medical devices, machinery, toys, lifts, radio equipment) AND must undergo third-party conformity assessment.
- **Article 6(2)**: The AI system falls within one of the **eight Annex III areas**: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services (including credit scoring), law enforcement, migration, and administration of justice.

The AI Act does **not** require that personal data be processed — it applies to AI systems regardless of whether they process personal data (Art. 2, Art. 3(50)-(51) definitions).

---

### 2. Where They Overlap

The two frameworks converge where an AI system **(a) processes personal data, (b) makes solely automated decisions with legal/similarly significant effects, AND (c) falls within an Annex III area or is a safety component under Annex I**. In these cases:

- **Human oversight**: Article 14 of the AI Act requires human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems. GDPR Art. 22(3) requires at minimum the right to obtain human intervention. The AI Act's requirement is broader and more structural (built into system design), while GDPR's is an individual right exercisable on request. The DLA Piper analysis notes that "meaningful intervention by a human being at a key stage of the AI system's decision-making process may be sufficient to ensure that the decision is no longer wholly automated for the purposes of article 22 GDPR" — meaning strong AI Act human oversight could potentially take a system **out of** Art. 22's scope.

- **Impact assessments**: GDPR Art. 35 requires a DPIA for processing that involves "systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects…based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects." The AI Act Art. 27 requires a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) for certain high-risk deployers. Art. 27(4) explicitly states that if obligations are "already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679…the fundamental rights impact assessment…shall complement that data protection impact assessment."

- **Transparency**: GDPR Art. 13(2)(f) requires information about "the existence of automated decision-making…meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences." The AI Act Art. 13 requires transparency and provision of information to deployers of high-risk systems.

- **Special category data**: GDPR Art. 22(4) prohibits solely automated decisions based on special categories of personal data (Art. 9(1)) unless explicit consent or substantial public interest applies. The AI Act separately prohibits certain uses of biometric categorisation (Art. 5(1)(g)) and emotion recognition in workplaces/education (Art. 5(1)(f)).

---

### 3. Cases Where GDPR Article 22 Applies BUT the EU AI Act Does NOT

These are scenarios where the AI Act's high-risk classification is not triggered, but Art. 22 still applies:

| Scenario | Why Art. 22 Applies | Why AI Act Does NOT Apply |
|---|---|---|
| **Automated pricing / e-commerce dynamic pricing** | Solely automated decision producing financial effects on individuals using personal data (browsing history, purchase patterns). | Not in Annex III (not credit scoring, not essential service). Not a safety component under Annex I. |
| **Automated content moderation on social media** | Solely automated decisions to remove content or suspend accounts — significant effects on freedom of expression. | Not listed in Annex III. Not a prohibited practice under Art. 5 unless it involves specific biometric or manipulative techniques. |
| **AI-driven marketing personalization that significantly affects individuals** | Profiling-based decisions about what offers, prices, or opportunities individuals see — can have similarly significant effects. | Marketing AI is not in Annex III. |
| **Automated insurance underwriting (non-life, non-health)** | Solely automated decisions on premiums or coverage with significant financial effects. | Only certain insurance AI falls under Annex III (essential private services). Some insurance AI may fall outside if not "essential." |
| **Automated tenant screening by private landlords** | Solely automated decisions on housing — significant effects. | Housing is not explicitly listed in Annex III (unlike credit scoring). |
| **Non-AI automated decision systems** | Art. 22 applies to any "automated processing" — not limited to AI. A simple rule-based algorithm (e.g., an Excel-based credit decision) could trigger Art. 22. | The AI Act only applies to "AI systems" as defined in Art. 3(1) — machine-based systems that infer how to generate outputs. Simple deterministic algorithms are not AI systems. |

**Key takeaway**: Art. 22 has a broader scope in terms of technology (any automated processing, not just AI) and covers many consumer-facing automated decisions that fall outside Annex III's eight categories.

---

### 4. Cases Where the EU AI Act Applies BUT GDPR Article 22 Does NOT

| Scenario | Why AI Act Applies | Why Art. 22 Does NOT Apply |
|---|---|---|
| **AI safety component in industrial machinery (no personal data)** | Art. 6(1): safety component of machinery under Annex I (Machinery Regulation). High-risk classification triggered. | No personal data processed → GDPR does not apply at all (Art. 2). |
| **AI system for predictive maintenance of critical infrastructure (no personal data)** | Annex III, point 2: critical infrastructure. | No personal data → GDPR out of scope. |
| **AI system with meaningful human in the loop** | The AI Act applies to the system regardless of human involvement. High-risk classification depends on the system's intended purpose, not the degree of automation. | Art. 22 only applies to **solely** automated decisions. If a qualified human reviews and makes the final decision, Art. 22 is not triggered. |
| **AI system that does not produce legal or similarly significant effects** | High-risk classification under Annex III does not depend on the effect on individuals. E.g., an AI system for biometric categorisation in a non-decisional context. | Art. 22 requires legal or similarly significant effects. |
| **AI system used in law enforcement (LED framework)** | Annex III, point 6: law enforcement. | GDPR Art. 22 is in the GDPR, which excludes "competent authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences" (Art. 2(2)(d)). These fall under the Law Enforcement Directive (EU) 2016/680 instead. |
| **AI system for migration, asylum, border control** | Annex III, point 7. | May involve personal data, but Art. 22 may be restricted under Art. 23 GDPR for important public interests. |

**Key takeaway**: The AI Act's high-risk classification is triggered by the **domain and function** of the AI system, not by whether it makes decisions about individuals. It captures many industrial, infrastructure, and public-sector uses where GDPR Art. 22 is either inapplicable (no personal data) or displaced by other legal frameworks.

---

### 5. Structural Differences in Approach

| Dimension | GDPR Article 22 | EU AI Act (High-Risk) |
|---|---|---|
| **Trigger** | Decision about an individual | Type/category of AI system |
| **Data requirement** | Must process personal data | No personal data requirement |
| **Automation level** | Must be **solely** automated | Applies regardless of automation level |
| **Effect threshold** | Legal or similarly significant effects | No effect threshold for classification |
| **Nature of obligation** | Individual right (can be waived by consent) | Regulatory compliance obligations (cannot be waived) |
| **Obligation bearer** | Data controller | Provider, deployer, importer, distributor |
| **Human oversight** | Right to human intervention on request | Built-in human oversight by design (Art. 14) |
| **Conformity assessment** | Not required (DPIA only) | Required for high-risk systems (Art. 43) |
| **Penalties** | Up to €20M or 4% global turnover | Up to €35M or 7% global turnover |

---

### 6. Practical Implications

1. **Dual compliance is common**: Many AI systems processing personal data for automated decisions in Annex III areas (credit scoring, employment, education, essential services) must comply with **both** frameworks simultaneously.

2. **Human oversight is the key hinge**: The level of human involvement determines Art. 22 applicability. The AI Act's Art. 14 human oversight requirements may, if implemented meaningfully, take a system outside Art. 22's scope — but this does not relieve the AI Act's own oversight obligations.

3. **Impact assessments can be integrated**: Art. 27(4) AI Act explicitly allows the FRIA to complement an existing GDPR DPIA, reducing duplication.

4. **Non-AI automated decisions remain GDPR-only**: Simple rule-based systems (not meeting the AI Act's definition of "AI system") that make solely automated significant decisions are regulated only by GDPR Art. 22.

5. **Industrial/non-personal AI is AI Act-only**: AI systems in machinery, infrastructure, or product safety that do not process personal data face AI Act obligations but not GDPR Art. 22.

6. **The AI Act fills GDPR's "human-in-the-loop" gap**: Even where Art. 22 does not apply (because there is a human in the loop), the AI Act may still require human oversight for high-risk systems — ensuring oversight is not merely formal but meaningful.

---

- CIDOB, "Humans in automated decision-making under the GDPR and AI Act," [cidob.org](https://www.cidob.org/en/publications/humans-automated-decision-making-under-gdpr-and-ai-act)
- Future of Privacy Forum, "Automated Decision-Making Under the GDPR" (May 2022), [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/FPF-ADM-Report-R2-singles.pdf)

question.question: Compare HIPAA's 'addressable' implementation specifications with SOC 2's flexibility in selecting controls to meet criteria. How do auditors evaluate each?
question.expected_answer: HIPAA's 'addressable' specifications (e.g. §164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption at rest, §164.312(e)(2)(ii) encryption in transit, §164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) testing/revision procedures) are not optional: a covered entity must assess whether the spec is reasonable and appropriate; if implemented, do so as written; if not, implement an equivalent alternative AND document the rationale. HHS auditors verify the documented analysis and any alternative measures. SOC 2 is criteria-based: the entity selects controls to meet each Trust Services Criterion; the auditor opines on whether the controls are suitably designed (Type 1) and operating effectively (Type 2). The flexibility is in the choice of controls, not in the criteria themselves. Both regimes allow tailoring but require documentation; HIPAA addressables require explicit justification for non-implementation, SOC 2 requires controls to be present and effective for every criterion in scope.

## HIPAA "Addressable" vs. SOC 2 Control Flexibility: A Comparative Analysis

### 1. The Nature of Flexibility

#### HIPAA: Addressable Implementation Specifications

Under **45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)**, HIPAA's Security Rule classifies implementation specifications as either **"Required"** or **"Addressable."** The critical — and frequently misunderstood — point is that **"addressable" does not mean "optional."** Rather, it imposes a structured, documented decision-making process:

When a specification is labeled "Addressable," the covered entity or business associate **must**:

1. **Assess** whether the specification is a *reasonable and appropriate safeguard* in its environment, considering the likely contribution to protecting ePHI (§ 164.306(d)(3)(i));
2. **If it is reasonable and appropriate** → implement it (§ 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(A));
3. **If it is NOT reasonable and appropriate** → **(a)** document *why* it is not reasonable and appropriate, **and** **(b)** implement an *equivalent alternative measure* if reasonable and appropriate (§ 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(B)).

This is further contextualized by the **"Flexibility of Approach"** provision at § 164.306(b), which allows entities to use *any* security measures that reasonably and appropriately implement the standards, considering:

- Size, complexity, and capabilities of the entity
- Technical infrastructure, hardware, and software security capabilities
- Costs of security measures
- Probability and criticality of potential risks to ePHI

**Examples of addressable specifications** include: automatic logoff (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iii)), encryption and decryption (§ 164.312(a)(2)(iv)), mechanism to authenticate ePHI (§ 164.312(c)(2)), integrity controls for transmission (§ 164.312(e)(2)(i)), transmission encryption (§ 164.312(e)(2)(ii)), contingency plan testing and revision (§ 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D)), and all workforce security and security awareness training specifications.

#### SOC 2: Points of Focus and Management Discretion

SOC 2 operates under a fundamentally different architecture. The **2017 Trust Services Criteria (TSP Section 100)** are organized around five trust services categories (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy), aligned to the 17 COSO principles. Each criterion is accompanied by **"points of focus"** — but critically:

> **"Use of the trust services criteria does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed."** (TSP § 100, ¶ .07)

The framework explicitly states:

- **"Some points of focus may not be suitable or relevant to the entity or to the engagement to be performed. In such situations, management may customize a particular point of focus or identify and consider other characteristics based on the specific circumstances of the entity."** (¶ .05)
- **"In some situations, management may consider additional points of focus based on the circumstances of the entity."** (¶ .06)

SOC 2's flexibility is broader and more principles-based: management selects which trust services categories to include, defines its own **service commitments and system requirements**, and then designs controls to meet the applicable criteria. There is no binary "required vs. addressable" taxonomy. Instead, the entire framework is built around the idea that controls must provide **reasonable assurance** that commitments and requirements are achieved.

---

### 2. Key Structural Differences

| Dimension | HIPAA Security Rule | SOC 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **Flexibility mechanism** | "Addressable" label on specific implementation specifications | Points of focus are illustrative, not mandatory; management defines commitments |
| **Is flexibility optional?** | No — addressable ≠ optional; a documented decision is mandatory | Yes — points of focus can be ignored if not relevant |
| **Burden when deviating** | Must document rationale AND implement equivalent alternative | Must still meet the underlying criterion; no specific documentation of deviation required |
| **Scope of flexibility** | Applies only to specifications labeled "Addressable" (~60% of Security Rule specs) | Applies to all criteria; management scopes categories and controls |
| **Guiding factors** | Statutory: size, complexity, cost, risk probability/criticality (§ 164.306(b)) | Entity-defined: service commitments, system requirements, risk assessment |
| **Prescribed controls** | Many specifications are "Required" with no flexibility (e.g., risk analysis, unique user ID, audit controls, contingency plan) | No prescribed controls; all controls are management-designed |

---

### 3. How Auditors Evaluate Each

#### HIPAA: OCR / Auditor Evaluation of Addressable Specifications

HIPAA compliance is evaluated through OCR investigations, compliance reviews (§ 160.308), and external audits. When evaluating addressable specifications, auditors examine:

1. **Documentation of the assessment**: Did the entity assess whether each addressable specification is reasonable and appropriate? The AHIMA External HIPAA Audit Readiness Toolkit explicitly requires: *"If an alternative measure (addressable) has been implemented, produce documentation of why the implementation specification is not a reasonable and appropriate safeguard and what equivalent alternative measure has been implemented."*

2. **Reasonableness of the decision**: Auditors evaluate whether the entity's determination — to implement, not implement, or substitute — was reasonable given the § 164.306(b) factors (size, complexity, cost, risk).

3. **Equivalence of alternatives**: If an alternative measure was implemented, auditors assess whether it provides *equivalent* protection. This is a substantive, not merely procedural, evaluation.

4. **Documentation retention**: All documentation must be retained for **6 years** (§ 164.316(b)(2)(i)).

**Enforcement reality**: The OCR has fined entities that treated addressable specifications as optional. As noted in recent guidance, "addressable specifications must still be implemented unless you can document why an alternative measure provides equivalent protection, or why the specification is not reasonable and appropriate for your environment." The 2024 proposed Security Rule updates further tighten expectations by introducing specific compliance time periods and requiring annual review of security measures.

#### SOC 2: Service Auditor Evaluation of Control Selection

In a SOC 2 examination, the service auditor evaluates:

1. **Description fairness**: Whether the description is presented in accordance with the description criteria (DC1–DC14). This includes whether management has disclosed any criteria that are not relevant and why (DC8).

2. **Suitability of design (Type 1 and Type 2)**: Whether controls are *suitably designed* to provide reasonable assurance that service commitments and system requirements would be achieved based on the applicable trust services criteria. The auditor does **not** check off a prescribed list — they evaluate whether the controls, as designed, address the risks that threaten achievement of commitments.

3. **Operating effectiveness (Type 2 only)**: Whether controls *operated effectively* over a defined period (typically 6–12 months). This requires evidence that controls were consistently applied.

4. **Points of focus as guidance, not checklist**: The service auditor uses points of focus as *characteristics* to assist evaluation — they are not mandatory requirements. The auditor considers whether management's control set, taken as a whole, meets each applicable criterion.

5. **Complementary controls**: The auditor evaluates whether complementary user entity controls and complementary subservice organization controls are properly identified and whether, in combination with service organization controls, they achieve the commitments.

**Critical distinction**: The SOC 2 auditor does not second-guess management's choice of which controls to implement, provided the controls collectively meet the criteria. The evaluation is outcome-oriented: do the controls provide reasonable assurance? This contrasts with HIPAA's more prescriptive approach, where the auditor evaluates whether the entity followed the correct decision-tree for each addressable specification.

---

### 4. Practical Implications

**HIPAA's approach** provides less genuine flexibility than it appears. Because the entity must either implement the specification or document an *equivalent* alternative, and because the OCR can challenge the equivalence determination, many entities simply implement all addressable specifications to reduce compliance risk. The documentation burden for deviating is substantial.

**SOC 2's approach** provides more genuine flexibility but places a heavier burden on management to design a coherent control environment from scratch. There is no "safe harbor" of implementing prescribed controls. The trade-off is that a well-designed SOC 2 control set can be more precisely tailored to the organization's actual risks and business model.

---

### 5. Summary Table: Auditor Evaluation

| Evaluation Aspect | HIPAA (OCR / External Auditor) | SOC 2 (Service Auditor) |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard for judgment** | Compliance with regulatory text | Reasonable assurance re: service commitments |
| **Checklist vs. principles** | Hybrid: Required specs are checklist; Addressable are principles-based with documentation | Fully principles-based; points of focus are illustrative |
| **Deviation consequence** | Must document and implement equivalent alternative | Must still meet the criterion; no specific deviation documentation required |
| **Evidence reviewed** | Policies, procedures, risk analysis, documentation of addressable decisions, alternative measure equivalence | Description, control design documentation, operating effectiveness evidence (Type 2) |
| **Opinion rendered** | Compliance determination / finding of violation | Opinion on description fairness, design suitability, and (Type 2) operating effectiveness |
| **Enforcement body** | HHS Office for Civil Rights | AICPA-licensed CPA firm (peer review) |

question.question: Compare NIST AI RMF's GOVERN function with SOC 2's CC1 control environment criteria. What organisational expectations do they share, and what's unique to each?
question.expected_answer: NIST AI RMF GOVERN (sub-categories 1–6) covers AI-specific policies/processes, accountability structures, workforce diversity/competence, engagement with affected communities, AI actor engagement, and third-party AI risk. SOC 2 CC1.1–CC1.5 cover the broader control environment: commitment to integrity and ethical values, board independence and oversight, organisational structures and reporting lines, attracting/developing/retaining competent individuals, and individual accountability. Shared: both require accountability structures, competent personnel, and policy frameworks. Unique to GOVERN: explicit treatment of AI-specific risks (bias, automation harms), engagement with affected communities/stakeholders beyond customers, and AI-actor (developer/deployer/user) role clarity. Unique to CC1: explicit board independence requirement and broader enterprise scope.

## Comparing NIST AI RMF's GOVERN Function and SOC 2's CC1 Control Environment

Both frameworks address **organisational governance as the foundational layer** for effective risk management, but they do so with different scopes, audiences, and specific expectations. Below is a structured comparison.

---

### What Is Unique to NIST AI RMF's GOVERN Function

1. **AI-Specific Risk Taxonomy and Lifecycle Scope.** GOVERN is explicitly designed to address risks across the entire AI lifecycle — from design and development through deployment, use, and decommissioning. It is "a cross-cutting function that is infused throughout AI risk management and enables the other functions" (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE). SOC 2's CC1 is technology-agnostic.

2. **AI System Inventory and Decommissioning.** GOVERN 1.6 requires "mechanisms to inventory AI systems" resourced according to risk priorities. GOVERN 1.7 requires "processes and procedures for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely." These are AI-specific operational controls with no direct CC1 analogue.

3. **Workforce Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Accessibility (DEIA).** GOVERN 3 is an entire category dedicated to ensuring "decision-making related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks throughout the lifecycle is informed by a diverse team (e.g., diversity of demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise, and backgrounds)" (GOVERN 3.1). This is a distinctive socio-technical requirement absent from CC1.

4. **Culture of Critical Thinking and Safety-First Mindset.** GOVERN 4.1 requires "organizational policies and practices to foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in the design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems to minimize potential negative impacts." This goes beyond general ethical standards to mandate a specific risk-aware culture tailored to AI.

5. **Integration of Trustworthy AI Characteristics.** GOVERN 1.2 requires that "the characteristics of trustworthy AI are integrated into organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices." These characteristics — valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed — are unique to the AI RMF and have no equivalent in CC1.

6. **Legal and Regulatory Requirements for AI.** GOVERN 1.1 specifically requires that "legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented." This is AI-domain-specific, whereas SOC 2's legal compliance considerations are framed generically.

7. **Human-AI Configuration Oversight.** GOVERN 3.2 requires policies and procedures to "define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems." This addresses the unique governance challenge of human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, and human-over-the-loop paradigms.

---

### What Is Unique to SOC 2's CC1 Control Environment

1. **COSO-Based Internal Control Framework.** CC1 is explicitly grounded in the COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework (2013), with five principles mapped directly from COSO. This gives CC1 a well-established, auditable structure rooted in financial reporting and internal control traditions that the AI RMF does not replicate.

2. **Explicit Board Independence Requirement.** CC1.2 requires that "the board of directors has sufficient members who are independent from management and objective in evaluations and decision making." The AI RMF GOVERN function emphasises leadership commitment but does not mandate structural independence of oversight bodies.

3. **Succession Planning.** CC1.4 requires that "senior management and the board of directors develop contingency plans for assignments of responsibility important for internal control." This operational continuity requirement has no direct parallel in GOVERN.

4. **Performance Measures, Incentives, and Rewards.** CC1.5 explicitly requires establishing "performance measures, incentives, and other rewards appropriate for responsibilities at all levels" and evaluating "excessive pressures" that might undermine internal control. GOVERN addresses accountability but does not prescribe incentive structures.

5. **Deviation Remediation.** CC1.1 requires that "deviations from the entity's expected standards of conduct are identified and remedied in a timely and consistent manner." While GOVERN implies monitoring and review, CC1 makes deviation handling an explicit, auditable control.

6. **Background Checks.** CC1.4's additional points of focus require the entity to "consider the background of potential and existing personnel, contractors, and vendor employees when determining whether to employ and retain the individuals." This personnel-screening dimension is absent from GOVERN.

7. **Service Auditor Examination Framework.** CC1 exists within the SOC 2 examination ecosystem, where a CPA (service auditor) opines on the suitability of design and operating effectiveness of controls. The AI RMF is voluntary guidance with no equivalent third-party attestation mechanism.

8. **Privacy-Specific Governance Additions.** CC1 includes additional points of focus for privacy engagements, such as establishing "structures, reporting lines, and authorities to support compliance with legal and contractual privacy requirements" (CC1.3) and a sanctions process for privacy violations (CC1.5).

---

### Summary

Both frameworks converge on the principle that **governance is foundational**: senior leadership must set the tone, roles must be documented, accountability must be enforced, and competence must be developed. However, **NIST AI RMF's GOVERN is AI-domain-specific, socio-technical, and lifecycle-oriented**, emphasising DEIA, safety-first culture, human-AI oversight, and trustworthy AI characteristics. **SOC 2's CC1 is internal-control-generic, COSO-grounded, and auditor-facing**, emphasising board independence, succession planning, incentive alignment, and formal deviation handling within an attestation framework.

An organisation deploying AI systems would be well-served to map CC1 as the baseline governance control environment and layer GOVERN on top for AI-specific risks — the two are complementary, not redundant.

## SR 11-7 vs. GDPR Article 28: Comparative Analysis for a Bank Using a SaaS AI Scoring Vendor

### 1. Foundational Differences in Purpose and Orientation

| Dimension | SR 11-7 (Vendor Models) | GDPR Article 28 (Processor Obligations) |
|-----------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Primary concern** | Safety and soundness — preventing financial loss from flawed model outputs | Protection of natural persons' rights and freedoms regarding their personal data |
| **Legal force** | Supervisory guidance (not enforceable rules per se), though violations of law or unsafe/unsound practices can trigger enforcement (SR 11-7 §I, fn.1) | Directly binding regulation with fines up to €20M or 4% of global annual turnover |
| **Who is regulated** | The banking organization (model user) | Both controller (bank) and processor (SaaS vendor) have direct statutory obligations |
| **Focus of oversight** | Model conceptual soundness, design, data, performance, ongoing monitoring | Lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, security, and data subject rights |

### 2. Key Differences

**A. Scope of Due Diligence**

- **SR 11-7** (§VII): The bank must develop an understanding of the vendor model's **conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance**. Even when components are proprietary, the bank cannot simply rely on the vendor's assurances — it must conduct its own validation, either internally or through outside parties. Ongoing monitoring and **outcome analysis** are required to verify the model remains fit for purpose.

- **GDPR Article 28(1)**: The controller (bank) must use only processors providing **"sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures"** such that processing meets GDPR requirements and protects data subject rights. The focus is on the processor's operational capabilities and security posture, not on the statistical validity of the model.

**B. Contractual Mandates**

- **SR 11-7**: Does not prescribe specific contract terms. The guidance is principles-based — the bank should ensure it has sufficient access and information to validate the model, but there is no statutory list of mandatory contract clauses.

- **GDPR Article 28(3)**: Mandates a **specific, enumerated list** of binding contract terms, including: documented instructions, confidentiality, Article 32 security measures, sub-processor rules, assistance with data subject rights and breach notification, deletion/return of data, and audit/inspection rights. This is a prescriptive, non-negotiable checklist.

**C. Sub-Processor / Fourth-Party Risk**

- **SR 11-7**: Silent on the mechanics of sub-vendor model risk. The guidance addresses vendor products generally but does not articulate a cascading liability or authorization framework for vendors who subcontract model components.

- **GDPR Article 28(2) & (4)**: Creates an explicit **cascading liability chain**. The processor must obtain prior specific or general written authorization before engaging another processor. The same data protection obligations must be flowed down contractually. If the sub-processor fails, the initial processor remains **fully liable** to the controller.

**D. Audit and Inspection Rights**

- **SR 11-7**: The bank is expected to validate vendor models, but the guidance acknowledges the practical challenge that vendors may withhold proprietary code, data, or methodology. There is no statutory right to compel access.

- **GDPR Article 28(3)(h)**: The processor must **"make available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance"** and **"allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections"** by the controller or its mandated auditor. This is a direct, enforceable obligation on the processor — the SaaS vendor cannot refuse on grounds of proprietary interest.

**E. Data Deletion / Portability at Termination**

- **SR 11-7**: Does not address data handling at contract termination.

- **GDPR Article 28(3)(g)**: The processor must, at the controller's choice, **delete or return all personal data** and delete existing copies unless EU or Member State law requires retention. This creates a concrete operational requirement for the bank's exit strategy from the SaaS vendor.

**F. Cross-Border Transfer**

- **SR 11-7**: No provisions on data residency or cross-border transfer.

- **GDPR Articles 44–46**: If the SaaS AI vendor processes EU personal data in a third country (e.g., a US-based cloud), the bank must ensure an **adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses (SCCs), binding corporate rules, or another valid transfer mechanism** is in place. This is entirely outside SR 11-7's scope.

### 3. Areas of Overlap for a Bank Using a SaaS AI Scoring Vendor Processing EU Personal Data

**Overlap 1: Due Diligence and Vendor Assessment**

Both frameworks require the bank to conduct upfront and ongoing vendor assessment. SR 11-7 demands validation of conceptual soundness and performance; GDPR Article 28(1) demands verification of sufficient technical and organizational guarantees. In practice, the bank's vendor risk management (VRM) process can serve both: the same vendor questionnaire and due diligence exercise can cover model methodology (SR 11-7) and data protection capabilities (GDPR), provided both dimensions are explicitly addressed.

**Overlap 2: Ongoing Monitoring**

SR 11-7 requires "ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis" of vendor models. GDPR Article 28(3)(h) requires the processor to contribute to audits and make compliance information available. Both create a continuous oversight obligation — the bank cannot treat either as a point-in-time exercise. A unified monitoring framework tracking both model performance metrics (drift, accuracy, fairness) and data protection KPIs (breach incidents, access logs, sub-processor changes) would satisfy both.

**Overlap 3: Documentation and Record-Keeping**

SR 11-7 emphasizes documentation for continuity of operations and tracking recommendations. GDPR Article 30 requires records of processing activities (ROPA) for both controller and processor. The bank's model inventory under SR 11-7 and its ROPA under GDPR should cross-reference each other — the AI scoring model should appear in both.

**Overlap 4: Security Measures**

SR 11-7 does not explicitly address cybersecurity, but model risk management implicitly requires securing model inputs, outputs, and the model itself. GDPR Article 28(3)(c) explicitly requires the processor to implement Article 32 security measures (encryption, pseudonymization, resilience, testing). For the SaaS AI vendor, these converge: securing the model API, training data, and inference outputs is both a model risk concern and a data protection requirement.

**Overlap 5: Governance and Accountability**

SR 11-7 requires clear roles and responsibilities, effective challenge by independent experts, and board-level visibility. GDPR Article 24 requires the controller to implement appropriate measures and **demonstrate** compliance (accountability principle). Both frameworks demand that the bank can prove — not just assert — that its vendor oversight is effective.

### 4. Practical Gaps the Bank Must Address

1. **Proprietary model access vs. audit rights**: SR 11-7 acknowledges the vendor may withhold code; GDPR Article 28(3)(h) gives the bank an enforceable right to audit. The bank should negotiate contract terms that leverage GDPR audit rights to also satisfy SR 11-7 validation needs — e.g., requiring the vendor to submit to independent third-party model audits where direct code access is restricted.

2. **Sub-processor mapping**: If the SaaS vendor uses sub-processors (e.g., cloud infrastructure, separate ML training pipelines), GDPR Article 28(2) requires authorization and flow-down. SR 11-7 does not address this, but the bank's model risk framework should extend to sub-vendor model components.

3. **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)**: GDPR Article 35 likely requires a DPIA because AI scoring involves "systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects" based on automated processing producing legal effects (credit decisions). SR 11-7 has no equivalent, but the DPIA's risk assessment can inform the model risk rating.

4. **International transfer mechanism**: If the SaaS vendor is US-based, the bank needs SCCs or another Article 46 transfer tool. This is purely a GDPR requirement with no SR 11-7 counterpart.

5. **Data deletion at exit**: GDPR Article 28(3)(g) requires a clear deletion/return plan. SR 11-7 does not address this, but model decommissioning should include purging EU personal data from vendor systems.

6. **AI literacy and transparency**: The EU AI Act (referenced in web results) adds AI literacy requirements (Article 4, effective February 2025) and transparency obligations that layer on top of both SR 11-7 and GDPR. The bank should treat these as additive.

### Summary Table

| Requirement Area | SR 11-7 | GDPR Art. 28 | Overlap? |
|-----------------|---------|-------------|----------|
| Vendor due diligence | ✅ | ✅ | **Yes** |
| Contractual mandates | ❌ (principles only) | ✅ (prescriptive list) | Partial |
| Ongoing monitoring | ✅ | ✅ | **Yes** |
| Audit/inspection rights | Implicit | ✅ (explicit, enforceable) | **Yes** |
| Sub-processor flow-down | ❌ | ✅ | Gap (SR 11-7 side) |
| Data deletion at termination | ❌ | ✅ | Gap (SR 11-7 side) |
| Cross-border transfer safeguards | ❌ | ✅ (Arts. 44–49) | Gap (SR 11-7 side) |
| DPIA / risk assessment | Model risk assessment | ✅ (Art. 35) | Partial |
| Model validation methodology | ✅ (core focus) | ❌ | Gap (GDPR side) |
| Data subject rights assistance | ❌ | ✅ (Art. 28(3)(e)) | Gap (SR 11-7 side) |

The two frameworks are complementary but not redundant. SR 11-7 focuses on whether the model *works correctly*; GDPR Article 28 focuses on whether personal data is *protected lawfully*. For a bank using a SaaS AI scoring vendor processing EU personal data, both must be satisfied, and the bank's vendor management program should be designed to address both frameworks in an integrated manner rather than treating them as separate compliance exercises.

question.question: What did the 2022 'Points of Focus' update to the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria add or refine regarding supply-chain and third-party risk?
question.expected_answer: The 2022 update did not change the criteria themselves but refined the Points of Focus accompanying the criteria, particularly around supply-chain and third-party risk. Specifically, CC9.2 (and related criteria) received refined points of focus addressing: identifying and assessing risks from vendors and business partners, considering the type of data and information shared, evaluating the vendor's commitments and system requirements, monitoring vendor performance against commitments, addressing identified risks through contracts or other means, communicating risk to relevant parties, and considering risks from sub-vendors. The update reflected post-SolarWinds concerns about supply-chain attacks and was paired with strengthened guidance on environmental and emerging threats.

## What the 2022 "Points of Focus" Update Added/Refined Regarding Supply-Chain and Third-Party Risk

The AICPA released the updated **TSP Section 100, *2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus — 2022)*** in Fall 2022. While the underlying Trust Services Criteria themselves did not change, the update introduced **new and expanded points of focus** across several criteria that significantly strengthened expectations around supply-chain, vendor, and third-party risk management. Here is what was added or refined:

---

### 1. CC3.2 — Risk Assessment: New Point of Focus on Third-Party Threat Analysis

**What was added:** A new point of focus titled **"Analyzes Threats and Vulnerabilities From Vendors, Business Partners, and Other Parties."**

> *"The entity's risk assessment process includes the analysis of potential threats and vulnerabilities arising from vendors providing goods and services, as well as threats and vulnerabilities arising from business partners, customers, and other third parties with access to the entity's information systems."*

This was a **new addition** in 2022. It explicitly requires that the entity's risk assessment process extend beyond internal threats to encompass the entire third-party ecosystem — including vendors, business partners, customers, and any other external parties with system access. This represents a meaningful expansion of the risk assessment lens to include supply-chain threat analysis as a distinct, named activity.

---

### 2. CC3.4 — Change Management / Risk Identification: New Point of Focus on Vendor Relationship Changes

**What was added:** A new point of focus titled **"Assesses Changes in Vendor and Business Partner Relationships."**

> *"The risk identification process considers changes in vendor and business partner relationships."*

This point of focus requires entities to treat changes in their vendor and business partner landscape as triggers for re-evaluating risk. Examples include onboarding new vendors, changes in the scope or nature of existing third-party services, or termination of relationships. This embeds third-party risk into the entity's ongoing change-management and risk-identification cadence.

---

### 3. CC9.2 — Risk Mitigation: Substantially Expanded Points of Focus for Vendor & Business Partner Management

CC9.2 itself states: *"The entity assesses and manages risks associated with vendors and business partners."* The 2022 update **significantly expanded** the points of focus under this criterion. The full set now includes:

| Point of Focus | What It Requires |
|---|---|
| **Establishes Requirements for Vendor and Business Partner Engagements** | Specific requirements covering (1) scope of services/product specs, (2) roles and responsibilities, (3) compliance requirements, and (4) service levels. |
| **Identifies Vulnerabilities** | Evaluates vulnerabilities arising from vendor/business partner relationships, including third-party access to IT systems and connections with third-party networks. |
| **Assesses Vendor and Business Partner Risks** | Inventories, tiers, and periodically assesses threats from vendors and business partners — **and their vendors/partners** (i.e., fourth-party/nth-party risk). Considers financial failure, security vulnerabilities, operational disruption, and regulatory non-compliance. |
| **Assigns Responsibility and Accountability for Managing Vendors and Business Partners** | Formal assignment of ownership for managing risks and changes associated with vendors and business partners. |
| **Establishes Communication Protocols for Vendors and Business Partners** | Defined communication and resolution protocols for service or product issues. |
| **Establishes Exception Handling Procedures From Vendors and Business Partners** | Formal exception-handling procedures for vendor-related service or product issues. |
| **Assesses Vendor and Business Partner Performance** | Periodic performance assessments, with frequency calibrated to risk. |
| **Implements Procedures for Addressing Issues Identified During Vendor and Business Partner Assessments** | Remediation procedures for issues found during assessments. |
| **Implements Procedures for Terminating Vendor and Business Partner Relationships** | Defined offboarding procedures, including safe return/removal of data from vendor systems. |

Additionally, **confidentiality-specific** and **privacy-specific** points of focus were added:

- **Confidentiality:** *"Obtains Confidentiality Commitments From Vendors and Business Partners"* and *"Assesses Compliance With Confidentiality Commitments of Vendors and Business Partners."*
- **Privacy:** *"Obtains Privacy Commitments From Vendors and Business Partners"* and *"Assesses Compliance With Privacy Commitments of Vendors and Business Partners."*

---

### 4. Description Criteria (DC) Implementation Guidance — Third-Party Access Disclosures

The 2022 update also revised the **Description Criteria implementation guidance** (DC2, DC5) to emphasize that service organizations should disclose:

- The nature of **third-party access and connectivity** to the service organization's system.
- The **functions or activities performed by third parties** within system components.
- The **process for addressing risks introduced by subservice organizations or other third parties**, including those with access to customer and employee data.

---

### Summary of the Shift

The 2022 Points of Focus update did not change the criteria themselves, but it **materially raised the bar** for what auditors and service organizations should consider when evaluating controls over third-party and supply-chain risk. The key themes are:

1. **Explicit inclusion** of vendor/business partner threat analysis in the risk assessment process (CC3.2).
2. **Ongoing monitoring** of changes in vendor relationships as a risk trigger (CC3.4).
3. **A comprehensive, lifecycle-based vendor risk management framework** — from onboarding requirements through performance monitoring to termination — with attention to fourth-party risk (CC9.2).
4. **Domain-specific third-party obligations** for confidentiality and privacy (CC9.2 add-ons).
5. **Enhanced disclosure expectations** around third-party access in the system description.

These changes reflect the AICPA's response to the growing reality that supply-chain and third-party compromises are among the most significant threats to service organizations' ability to meet their service commitments and system requirements.

**Sources:**
- AICPA, *TSP Section 100 — 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus — 2022)*
- Linford & Co., ["Trust Services Criteria (TSCs): SOC 2 Audit Guidance"](https://linfordco.com/blog/trust-services-critieria-principles-soc-2)
- Schellman, ["A Breakdown of the Latest SOC 2 Guidance Revisions (October 2022)"](https://www.schellman.com/blog/latest-soc-2-guidance-revisions-october-2022)
- Barr Advisory, ["SOC 2 Compliance: What's New in the Revised Points of Focus?"](https://www.barradvisory.com/resource/whats-new-with-soc-2)
- EY, ["To the Point: AICPA revises guidance on applying its Trust Services Criteria"](https://www.ey.com/content/dam/ey-unified-site/ey-com/en-us/technical/accountinglink/documents/ey-ttp17549-221us-11-02-2022.pdf)

question.expected_answer: NIST AI 600-1 (Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024) supplements AI RMF 1.0 with 12 categories of risk unique to or exacerbated by generative AI: CBRN/Nuclear information availability, confabulation, dangerous/violent/hateful content, data privacy, environmental impact, harmful bias, human-AI configuration, information integrity, information security, intellectual property, obscene/degrading/abusive content, and value-chain/component integration. It maps each risk to suggested actions across all four AI RMF functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and provides ~200 actionable subcategory items. The Profile is voluntary and complements (not replaces) AI RMF 1.0.
