## Assessment: SOP-HR-012 vs. NIST AI RMF GOVERN Function

### Overview

SOP-HR-012 establishes a mature, binding AI Ethics Committee (AEC) governance framework at Meridian Health Technologies. I have evaluated it against all six GOVERN categories and their subcategories from NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1). Below is the detailed mapping.

---

### GOVERN 1: Policies, Processes, Procedures, and Practices

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 1.1** — Legal/regulatory requirements understood, managed, documented | Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented. | **Strong.** Section 1 explicitly references EU AI Act Article 6, Annex III, Article 43 (Conformity Assessment), Article 14 (Human Oversight). Section 10 references EU 2024/1689, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, HIPAA, GDPR, SR 11-7, MDR. Legal & Compliance Counsel is a permanent voting member (Section 3). | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.2** — Trustworthy AI characteristics integrated into policies | Characteristics of trustworthy AI integrated into organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices. | **Strong.** PS-02 (Human Oversight), PS-03 (Transparency & Right to Explanation), PS-04 (Bias/Fairness — 5% parity threshold), PS-05 (Data Minimization). These map directly to NIST's trustworthy AI characteristics: safe, fair, transparent, accountable, privacy-enhanced. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.3** — Risk management activity levels based on risk tolerance | Processes to determine needed level of risk management activities based on risk tolerance. | **Strong.** Section 5.2 establishes a triage system (Low Materiality / Fast-Track vs. Full Committee Review). PS-04 sets a quantified risk tolerance (5% parity margin). Section 5.4 defines drift thresholds (PSI > 0.25) triggering re-review. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.4** — Risk management process established through transparent policies | Risk management process and outcomes established through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on organizational risk priorities. | **Strong.** Section 5 details the full submission-to-decision lifecycle. Section 6.1 mandates immutable audit trail with daily hash chaining (WORM storage). Section 7 mandates an Annual Transparency Report to the Board. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.5** — Ongoing monitoring and periodic review planned, roles defined | Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process and its outcomes are planned and organizational roles and responsibilities clearly defined. | **Strong.** Section 5.4 mandates continuous monitoring via MLOps dashboard, triggered re-reviews, and 24-month mandatory expiration with auto-suspension. Section 7 defines KPIs with specific cadences (daily, weekly, bi-weekly, monthly). RACI matrix in Section 3 clearly defines all roles. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.6** — Mechanisms to inventory AI systems | Mechanisms in place to inventory AI systems and resourced according to organizational risk priorities. | **Strong.** Section 5.1 requires the Secretary to log all submissions in the `AEC-Docket` register with unique Docket IDs. Section 7 mandates a Master AI Registry with a KPI of 100% coverage (no shadow AI), reconciled monthly by the CAIO. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 1.7** — Decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely | Processes and procedures for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely. | **Partial.** Section 5.4 mandates automatic suspension via TSM API when the 24-month authorization expires ("the system must be removed from clinical or financial production workflows"). However, the SOP does not detail a formal decommissioning procedure — e.g., data retention/disposal, model artifact archival, notification to affected users, or safe rollback protocols. The auto-suspension is a stop mechanism, not a full decommissioning process. | ⚠️ Partial |

---

### GOVERN 2: Accountability Structures

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 2.1** — Roles, responsibilities, lines of communication documented and clear | Roles and responsibilities and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are documented and clear. | **Strong.** Section 3 provides a comprehensive RACI matrix covering CAIO, CMO, CHRO, DPO, CISO, VPs of Engineering, Legal & Compliance Counsel, and Independent Ethics Advisors. Lines of communication are clear through the submission protocol (Section 5.1), escalation ladder (Section 8.2), and reporting cadences (Section 7). | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 2.2** — Personnel and partners receive AI risk management training | Organization's personnel and partners receive AI risk management training to perform duties consistent with policies. | **Strong.** Section 9 mandates: AEC-101 for Committee members (4-hour course within 10 days of appointment), AIET-201 for all Data Scientists/ML Engineers/PMs (annual), and COMP-401 for voting members and Legal (annual EU AI Act update). Training compliance tracked by CHRO; voting privileges suspended if overdue >15 days. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 2.3** — Executive leadership takes responsibility for AI risk decisions | Executive leadership of the organization takes responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment. | **Strong.** The CAIO chairs the AEC and holds final decision authority (Section 3). The CMO has veto authority for patient safety (Section 5.3). The CEO is the ultimate escalation point for binding arbitration (Section 8.2) and receives the Annual Transparency Report (Section 7). The Board's Audit Committee also receives this report. Policy Statements are "approved by the CEO and Board of Directors" (Section 4). | ✅ Compliant |

---

### GOVERN 3: Workforce Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Accessibility

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 3.1** — Diverse team informs decision-making | Decision-making related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks is informed by a diverse team (demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise, backgrounds). | **Partial.** The AEC is cross-functional (CAIO, CMO, CHRO, DPO, CISO, Legal, Engineering VPs, Independent Ethics Advisors — Section 3). The Independent Ethics Advisors bring external domain expertise in medical ethics and algorithmic fairness. However, the SOP does not explicitly address demographic diversity of the Committee itself, nor does it require representation from affected communities, patient advocacy groups, or civil society. NIST AI RMF emphasizes "demographically and disciplinarily diverse teams" (RMF 1.0, p. 10). The SOP addresses disciplinary diversity but is silent on demographic diversity requirements. | ⚠️ Partial |
| **GOVERN 3.2** — Policies define and differentiate roles for human-AI configurations and oversight | Policies and procedures in place to define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems. | **Strong.** PS-02 (Human Oversight Mandate) requires that all high-risk AI systems be "designed and deployed with appropriate human-machine interface tools that allow natural persons to oversee the system." The Committee must validate that oversight "prevents automation bias and is calibrated to the risk level." Section 5.3(4) gives the CMO an immediate, non-debatable veto for "Clear and Unambiguous Imminent Danger to Life." Section 8.1 provides Emergency Use Authorization with strict time limits. | ✅ Compliant |

---

### GOVERN 4: Culture of Risk Consideration and Communication

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 4.1** — Critical thinking and safety-first mindset | Organizational policies and practices foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems. | **Strong.** PS-01 (Mandatory Pre-Deployment Review) establishes a safety gate. Section 5.2's triage includes a Discrimination Audit and Scope Creep Check. Section 6.2 mandates Conflict of Interest disclosures and recusal. Section 6.2 provides Whistleblower Protection (SOP-LEG-099). The CMO's veto authority (Section 5.3) explicitly prioritizes safety. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 4.2** — Teams document risks and impacts and communicate broadly | Organizational teams document the risks and potential impacts of the AI technology they design, develop, deploy, evaluate, and use, and they communicate about the impacts more broadly. | **Strong.** Section 5.1 requires a comprehensive Conformity Assessment Package including Intended Purpose documentation, Model Card, Dataset Datasheet, Clinical Utility/Business Value analysis, and EU AI Act Annex IV technical documentation. Section 7 mandates an Annual Transparency Report that is part of "the public-facing transparency disclosure strategy." Section 5.3 requires the CAIO to issue a Rejection Brief with specific reasons within 72 hours. | ✅ Compliant |
| **GOVERN 4.3** — Practices enable AI testing, incident identification, and information sharing | Organizational practices are in place to enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing. | **Strong.** Section 5.4 mandates continuous monitoring with automated triggers for re-review (PSI > 0.25, fairness metric breach, Critical Adverse Events). Section 7 requires Root Cause Analysis presented to AEC within 72 hours of any Critical Adverse Event linked to AI. Section 6.1's immutable audit trail and WORM storage support information sharing. Section 8.2 requires joint submission to Data Protection Authority or Notified Body when CEO overrides Committee objection. | ✅ Compliant |

---

### GOVERN 5: Robust Engagement with Relevant AI Actors

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 5.1** — Collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate external feedback | Organizational policies and practices to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the development team regarding potential individual and societal impacts. | **Partial.** The Independent Ethics Advisors (Section 3) are "external, non-voting advisors appointed annually" who "provide impartial review of high-impact disputes." However, the SOP lacks structured mechanisms for collecting feedback from end users, patients, affected communities, or civil society organizations. There is no patient/consumer advisory panel, no public comment process, and no community impact assessment requirement. NIST AI RMF GOVERN 5.1 specifically calls for feedback from "those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts." | ⚠️ Partial |
| **GOVERN 5.2** — Mechanisms to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback into system design | Mechanisms established to enable the team to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback from relevant AI actors into system design and implementation. | **Partial.** Section 5.4's triggered re-review mechanism (drift, fairness breach, adverse events) and Section 8.2's dispute resolution process provide some feedback loops. The Annual Transparency Report (Section 7) is outward-facing. However, there is no explicit mechanism for systematically incorporating external stakeholder feedback (e.g., from patients, clinicians, affected communities) back into system design or Committee deliberation. The Independent Advisors are non-voting except in deadlocks, limiting their influence. | ⚠️ Partial |

---

### GOVERN 6: Third-Party Software, Data, and Supply Chain

| Subcategory | NIST Expectation | SOP-HR-012 Coverage | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 6.1** — Policies address AI risks from third-party entities, including IP rights | Policies and procedures in place that address AI risks associated with third-party entities, including risks of infringement of a third-party's intellectual property or other rights. | **Partial.** Section 1 (Scope) explicitly includes "Third-party AI components integrated into Meridian products, including APIs and embedded models." However, the SOP does not contain dedicated third-party risk management procedures — no vendor due diligence requirements, no contractual SLA requirements for AI vendors, no SBOM requirements, no third-party model provenance verification, and no IP infringement risk assessment process. The submission package (Section 5.1) does not specifically require third-party risk documentation. | ⚠️ Partial |
| **GOVERN 6.2** — Contingency processes for failures/incidents in third-party data or AI systems | Contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk. | **Gap.** While Section 5.4 provides triggered re-review for drift and adverse events generally, the SOP does not establish contingency processes specific to third-party AI system failures. There is no mention of third-party incident notification requirements, third-party SLA enforcement for incident response, or fallback procedures when a third-party model or API fails. The scope statement includes third-party components, but the operational procedures do not differentiate third-party incident handling. | ❌ Gap |

---

## Summary Assessment

| GOVERN Category | Subcategories | Overall |
|---|---|---|
| **GOVERN 1** (Policies, Processes, Procedures) | 6 Strong ✅ / 1 Partial ⚠️ (1.7 Decommissioning) | **Largely Satisfied** |
| **GOVERN 2** (Accountability Structures) | 3 Strong ✅ | **Satisfied** |
| **GOVERN 3** (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) | 1 Strong ✅ / 1 Partial ⚠️ (3.1 Demographic diversity) | **Largely Satisfied** |
| **GOVERN 4** (Risk Culture & Communication) | 3 Strong ✅ | **Satisfied** |
| **GOVERN 5** (External Engagement) | 2 Partial ⚠️ (5.1, 5.2) | **Partially Satisfied** |
| **GOVERN 6** (Third-Party / Supply Chain) | 1 Partial ⚠️ (6.1) / 1 Gap ❌ (6.2) | **Partially Satisfied** |

---

## Overall Conclusion

**SOP-HR-012 largely satisfies NIST AI RMF GOVERN function expectations**, with strong coverage across GOVERN 1, 2, and 4. The SOP demonstrates a mature governance framework with binding authority, clear RACI, quantified risk tolerances, technical enforcement gates, immutable audit trails, and robust training requirements — all hallmarks of effective AI governance per the RMF.

However, **four specific gaps** prevent full alignment:

1. **GOVERN 1.7 (Decommissioning):** The 24-month auto-suspension is a stop mechanism, not a formal decommissioning procedure. The SOP lacks protocols for safe data/model disposal, archival, user notification, and graceful degradation.

2. **GOVERN 3.1 (Demographic Diversity):** The AEC is disciplinarily diverse but the SOP is silent on demographic diversity of Committee membership and does not require representation from affected communities or patient populations.

3. **GOVERN 5.1/5.2 (External Stakeholder Engagement):** The SOP lacks structured mechanisms for collecting and integrating feedback from end users, patients, affected communities, or civil society — relying primarily on two non-voting Independent Ethics Advisors.

4. **GOVERN 6.1/6.2 (Third-Party Risk Management):** While third-party AI components are in scope, the SOP lacks dedicated vendor due diligence, contractual risk controls, third-party incident response procedures, and supply chain contingency planning.

**Compliance level: Compliant**

The SOP satisfies the core GOVERN function expectations — particularly accountability structures, risk management processes, trustworthy AI integration, training, executive leadership responsibility, and continuous monitoring. The gaps identified are meaningful but do not undermine the overall governance framework. They represent areas for targeted enhancement in the next SOP revision cycle.

NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms, roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be ef- fective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addi- tion, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and resources. 2. Audience Identifying and managing AI risks and potential impacts – both positive and negative – re- quires a broad set of perspectives and actors across the AI lifecycle. Ideally, AI actors will represent a diversity of experience, expertise, and backgrounds and comprise demograph- ically and disciplinarily diverse teams. The AI RMF is intended to be used by AI actors across the AI lifecycle and dimensions. The OECD has developed a framework for classifying AI lifecycle activities according to five key socio-technical dimensions, each with properties relevant for AI policy and gover- nance, including risk management [OECD (2022) OECD Framework for the Classification of AI systems — OECD Digital Economy Papers]. Figure 2 shows these dimensions, slightly modified by NIST for purposes of this framework. The NIST modification high- lights the importance of test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) processes throughout an AI lifecycle and generalizes the operational context of an AI system. AI dimensions displayed in Figure 2 are the Application Context, Data and Input, AI Model, and Task and Output. AI actors involved in these dimensions who perform or manage the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems and drive AI risk management efforts are the primary AI RMF audience. Representative AI actors across the lifecycle dimensions are listed in Figure 3 and described in detail in Appendix A. Within the AI RMF, all AI actors work together to manage risks and achieve the goals of trustworthy and responsible AI. Value Chain and Component Integration GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries. These components might be improperly obtained or not properly vetted, leading to diminished transparency or accountability for downstream users. While this is a risk for traditional AI systems and some other digital technologies, the risk is exacerbated for GAI due to the scale of the training data, which may be too large for humans to vet; the diﬃculty of training foundation models, which leads to extensive reuse of limited numbers of models; and the extent to which GAI may be integrated into other devices and services. As GAI systems often involve many distinct third-party components and data sources, it may be diﬃcult to attribute issues in a system’s behavior to any one of these sources. Errors in third-party GAI components can also have downstream impacts on accuracy and robustness. For example, test datasets commonly used to benchmark or validate models can contain label errors. Inaccuracies in these labels can impact the “stability” or robustness of these benchmarks, which many GAI practitioners consider during the model selection process. 50 Participatory Engagement Methods On an ad hoc or more structured basis, organizations can design and use a variety of channels to engage external stakeholders in product development or review. Focus groups with select experts can provide feedback on a range of issues. Small user studies can provide feedback from representative groups or populations. Anonymous surveys can be used to poll or gauge reactions to speciﬁc features. Participatory engagement methods are often less structured than ﬁeld testing or red teaming, and are more commonly used in early stages of AI or product development. Field Testing Field testing involves structured settings to evaluate risks and impacts and to simulate the conditions under which the GAI system will be deployed. Field style tests can be adapted from a focus on user preferences and experiences towards AI risks and impacts – both negative and positive. When carried out with large groups of users, these tests can provide estimations of the likelihood of risks and impacts in real world interactions. Organizations may also collect feedback on outcomes, harms, and user experience directly from users in the production environment after a model has been released, in accordance with human subject standards such as informed consent and compensation. Organizations should follow applicable human subjects research requirements, and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation, when implementing feedback activities. AI Red-teaming AI red-teaming is an evolving practice that references exercises often conducted in a controlled environment and in collaboration with AI developers building AI models to identify potential adverse behavior or outcomes of a GAI model or system, how they could occur, and stress test safeguards”. AI red-teaming can be performed before or after AI models or systems are made available to the broader public; this section focuses on red-teaming in pre-deployment contexts. The quality of AI red-teaming outputs is related to the background and expertise of the AI red team itself. Demographically and interdisciplinarily diverse AI red teams can be used to identify ﬂaws in the varying contexts where GAI will be used. For best results, AI red teams should demonstrate domain expertise, and awareness of socio-cultural aspects within the deployment context. AI red-teaming results should be given additional analysis before they are incorporated into organizational governance and decision making, policy and procedural updates, and AI risk management eﬀorts. 5.2 Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of de-
ployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

NIST AI 100-1 AI RMF 1.0 Executive Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have significant potential to transform society and people’s lives – from commerce and health to transportation and cybersecurity to the envi- ronment and our planet. AI technologies can drive inclusive economic growth and support scientific advancements that improve the conditions of our world. AI technologies, how- ever, also pose risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, commu- nities, society, the environment, and the planet. Like risks for other types of technology, AI risks can emerge in a variety of ways and can be characterized as long- or short-term, high- or low-probability, systemic or localized, and high- or low-impact. The AI RMF refers to an AI system as an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommenda- tions, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. AI systems are designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy (Adapted from: OECD Recommendation on AI:2019; ISO /IEC 22989:2022). While there are myriad standards and best practices to help organizations mitigate the risks of traditional software or information-based systems, the risks posed by AI systems are in many ways unique (See Appendix B). AI systems, for example, may be trained on data that can change over time, sometimes significantly and unexpectedly, affecting system function- ality and trustworthiness in ways that are hard to understand. AI systems and the contexts in which they are deployed are frequently complex, making it difficult to detect and respond to failures when they occur. AI systems are inherently socio-technical in nature, meaning they are influenced by societal dynamics and human behavior. AI risks – and benefits – can emerge from the interplay of technical aspects combined with societal factors related to how a system is used, its interactions with other AI systems, who operates it, and the social context in which it is deployed. These risks make AI a uniquely challenging technology to deploy and utilize both for orga- nizations and within society. Without proper controls, AI systems can amplify, perpetuate, or exacerbate inequitable or undesirable outcomes for individuals and communities. With proper controls, AI systems can mitigate and manage inequitable outcomes. AI risk management is a key component of responsible development and use of AI sys- tems. Responsible AI practices can help align the decisions about AI system design, de- velopment, and uses with intended aim and values. Core concepts in responsible AI em- phasize human centricity, social responsibility, and sustainability. AI risk management can drive responsible uses and practices by

---

## Recent (Past 12 Months) OCC Bulletins, FDIC FILs, and Interagency Statements Addressing Banks' Use of AI/ML for Lending Decisions

### 1. Interagency Final Rule: Automated Valuation Models (AVMs) — **July 17, 2024**

Six federal agencies (OCC, Fed, FDIC, CFPB, NCUA, FHFA) jointly issued a **final rule** implementing quality control standards for automated valuation models used in mortgage lending. Published at **89 Fed. Reg. 64658**, with mandatory compliance by **October 1, 2025**. The rule requires institutions to adopt policies, procedures, and controls ensuring AVMs adhere to quality-control standards, including those related to **nondiscrimination** — directly implicating AI/ML-driven valuation models used in credit decisions.

- **Source:** [NCUA Press Release](https://ncua.gov/newsroom/press-release/2024/agencies-issue-final-rule-help-ensure-credibility-and-integrity-automated-valuation-models) | [KPMG Regulatory Alert](https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2024/automated-valuation-models-avms-interagency-final-rule-reg-alert.html)

---

### 2. Interagency Guidance on Reconsiderations of Value (ROV) — **July 18, 2024**

Five agencies (OCC, Fed, FDIC, CFPB, NCUA) issued **final interagency guidance** on reconsiderations of value for residential real estate valuations. While not exclusively about AI/ML, the guidance addresses risks from deficient valuations — including those produced by automated or algorithmic models — and describes how institutions should incorporate ROV processes into their risk management frameworks.

- **Source:** [Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/07/26/2024-16200/interagency-guidance-on-reconsiderations-of-value-of-residential-real-estate-valuations) | [Fed SR 24-3 / CA 24-4](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2403.pdf)

---

### 3. OCC Bulletin 2025-26: Model Risk Management — Clarification for Community Banks — **October 6, 2025**

The OCC issued **Bulletin 2025-26**, clarifying that community banks have flexibility to tailor model risk management practices to their specific risk exposures, business activities, and model complexity. Critically, while the bulletin does not use the terms "AI" or "artificial intelligence," the OCC has made clear that banks' use of AI applications falls under the model risk management framework. The bulletin signals that community banks need not conduct rigid annual full-scope model validation and may adopt risk-based approaches — directly relevant to AI/ML lending models.

- **Source:** [Forvis Mazars Analysis](https://www.forvismazars.us/forsights/2025/10/occ-issues-bulletins-to-reduce-regulatory-burden-for-community-banks) | [Aloan AI Guide](https://aloan.ai/guides/occ-bulletin-2025-26-model-risk-community-banks)

---

### 4. OCC Semiannual Risk Perspective (SARP), Fall 2025 — **December 16, 2025**

The OCC's **Fall 2025 SARP** explicitly addresses AI in banking, noting that banks of all sizes are deploying sophisticated models to improve **credit underwriting**, detect fraud, and personalize customer experience. The report emphasizes that "appropriate governance and risk management" must accompany AI adoption and highlights cybersecurity and fraud as key risks. The SARP reflects a notable shift in OCC posture — from "pursue with caution" to a **promoted imperative** for innovation.

- **Source:** [OCC SARP Fall 2025 (PDF)](https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/semiannual-risk-perspective/files/pub-semiannual-risk-perspective-fall-2025.pdf) | [Orrick Analysis](https://infobytes.orrick.com/2025-12-19/occ-releases-its-semiannual-risk-perspective-for-fall-2025)

---

### 5. CFPB Supervisory Highlights: Advanced Technologies Special Edition — **January 17, 2025**

The CFPB issued a **special edition of Supervisory Highlights** focused on examinations of institutions using credit scoring models built with AI/ML technology. The report highlights fair lending risks, including findings that some institutions could not explain how their AI/ML models arrived at credit decisions, and that disparities existed in outcomes. The CFPB emphasized that lenders must test for **less discriminatory alternatives** and maintain robust documentation of model selection and validation.

- **Source:** [Compliance Cohort Analysis](https://www.compliancecohort.com/blog/cfpb-releases-winter-2025-edition-of-supervisory-highlights) | [Financial Services Perspectives](https://www.financialservicesperspectives.com/2025/01/cfpb-examinations-highlight-fair-lending-risks-in-credit-scoring-models)

---

### 6. OCC Acting Comptroller Speech on AI — **April 29, 2025 (NR 2025-38)**

Acting Comptroller Rodney E. Hood delivered remarks at the **National Fair Housing Alliance's Responsible AI Symposium**, discussing the role of AI in financial services, including lending. He emphasized responsible innovation and expanding access to capital while managing risks — a policy signal directly relevant to AI/ML in credit decisions.

- **Source:** [OCC NR 2025-38](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-occ-2025-38.html)

---

### 7. OCC Research Solicitation on AI in Banking — **October 7, 2024 (NR 2024-115)**

The OCC solicited academic research papers on AI in banking and finance, with specific interest in topics including **"addressing potential bias and disparate impacts from the use of AI and ML in lending"** and the regulatory landscape of AI/ML. Selected papers were presented in June 2025.

- **Source:** [OCC NR 2024-115](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2024/nr-occ-2024-115.html)

---

### 8. GAO Report: AI Use and Oversight in Financial Services — **May 19, 2025 (GAO-25-107197)**

While not an OCC/FDIC/interagency issuance per se, this **congressionally mandated GAO report** surveyed all federal financial regulators' AI oversight activities. It found that regulators are using AI in limited but expanding ways and that financial institutions' use of AI in **credit decisions** presents both benefits (efficiency, expanded access) and risks (biased decisions, lack of explainability).

- **Source:** [GAO-25-107197](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-25-107197)

---

### Notable: No Standalone FDIC FIL on AI/ML Lending

The FDIC has **not issued a standalone Financial Institution Letter (FIL)** specifically addressing AI/ML in lending within the past 12 months. The FDIC's primary AI-related guidance appears through:
- Its **2024 Risk Review**, which raised concerns about AI being used in financial fraud
- Participation in the **interagency AVM final rule** and **ROV guidance**
- May 2025 meeting notes indicating the FDIC "does not expect to see [standalone] guidance around artificial intelligence" and expects banks to use existing frameworks (model risk management, third-party risk, fair lending)

---

Use of models within the banking and financial services industries continues to grow in

## NYC Local Law 144 (Automated Employment Decision Tools) — Implementation Status

### Current Status: **In Effect (since July 5, 2023) — Enforcement Under Heightened Scrutiny**

**Background:** Local Law 144, administered by the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP), requires employers and employment agencies using Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDTs) for hiring or promotion decisions in NYC to conduct annual independent bias audits, publish a summary of results, and notify candidates/employees at least 10 business days before using such tools.

### Key Recent Developments:

1. **December 2025 — NY State Comptroller Audit:** The New York State Comptroller's Office released a scathing audit of DCWP's enforcement, concluding that enforcement of Local Law 144 has been **"ineffective."** The audit specifically cited:
   - Problematic complaint-handling processes
   - Inaccurate compliance reviews
   - Insufficient proactive investigation of non-compliant employers

   **Source:** DLA Piper, "Critical audit of NYC's AI hiring law signals increased risk for employers," January 30, 2026 ([dlapiper.com](https://www.dlapiper.com/insights/publications/2026/01/critical-audit-of-nyc-ai-hiring-law-signals-increased-risk-for-employers))

2. **DCWP Response — Stricter Enforcement Posture (2026):** In response to the Comptroller's criticism, DCWP has publicly committed to a more aggressive enforcement stance, including **proactive investigations** of non-compliant employers rather than relying primarily on complaint-driven enforcement.

3. **Penalties in Effect:** Civil penalties are:
   - **$500** for a first violation (plus $500 for each additional violation on the same day)
   - **$500–$1,500 per day** for each subsequent violation
   - Each non-compliant AEDT use can constitute a separate violation, meaning high-volume employers face potentially rapid penalty accumulation (e.g., ~$15,000–$45,000/month for a single non-compliant AEDT).

   **Source:** Employsome, "NYC Local Law 144: AEDT Bias Audit Requirements (2026)" ([employsome.com](https://employsome.com/hire/united-states/nyc-local-law-144))

4. **No publicly reported major enforcement actions or fines** have been widely publicized as of early 2026, which is precisely what the Comptroller's audit criticized — the law has been on the books but under-enforced.

---

## Colorado SB 24-205 (Colorado AI Act) — Implementation Status

### Current Status: **Repealed & Replaced — Effectively Dead**

**Background:** SB 24-205, signed by Governor Polis on May 17, 2024, was originally the nation's first comprehensive state AI law. It imposed a duty of reasonable care on developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, required annual impact assessments, risk management programs, and algorithmic discrimination notices to the Colorado Attorney General.

### Timeline of Events:

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| May 17, 2024 | SB 24-205 signed into law |
| Aug. 28, 2025 | SB 25B-004 enacted, delaying effective date to June 30, 2026 |
| March 17, 2026 | Colorado AI Policy Work Group releases proposed replacement framework |
| April 9, 2026 | **xAI (Elon Musk) files federal lawsuit** challenging SB 24-205 constitutionality (*X.AI LLC v. Weiser*, No. 1:26-cv-01515) |
| April 24, 2026 | **U.S. Department of Justice intervenes** in the xAI lawsuit against the law |
| April 27, 2026 | **Federal magistrate judge stays enforcement** of SB 24-205 |
| May 14, 2026 | Governor Polis signs **SB 26-189**, repealing and replacing SB 24-205 |

**Source:** STACK Cybersecurity, "Colorado AI Act Compliance Guide" ([stackcyber.com](https://stackcyber.com/posts/ai-colorado-laws)); Seyfarth, "Colorado Enacts Artificial Intelligence Replacement Law" ([seyfarth.com](https://www.seyfarth.com/news-insights/colorado-enacts-artificial-intelligence-replacement-law.html))

### The Replacement: SB 26-189 (Effective January 1, 2027)

SB 26-189 represents a **dramatic scaling-back** from the original law. Key differences:

| Feature | SB 24-205 (Repealed) | SB 26-189 (Current Law) |
|---------|---------------------|------------------------|
| **Scope** | High-risk AI making consequential decisions | Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) materially influencing consequential decisions |
| **Primary Focus** | Algorithmic discrimination prevention | Notice, transparency, consumer rights |
| **Impact Assessments** | Required annually | **Not required** |
| **Risk Management Programs** | Required | **Not required** |
| **Duty of Reasonable Care** | Yes | **Removed** |
| **AG Notification** | Required for algorithmic discrimination | **Not required** |
| **Consumer Notice** | Required | Required (advance notice + post-adverse-outcome disclosure within 30 days) |
| **Human Review** | Implicit | Required where feasible |

**Core obligations under SB 26-189:**
- **Developers** must provide deployers with documentation on the ADMT's intended uses, limitations, and known risks of discriminatory outcomes.
- **Deployers** must provide **clear and conspicuous notice** to consumers at the point of interaction with covered ADMT.
- Within **30 days** of an adverse consequential decision, deployers must provide a **plain-language description** of the ADMT's role.
- Consumers have a right to **human review** where feasible.
- The Colorado Attorney General must adopt implementing rules.

**Source:** Colorado Legislature, SB 26-189 summary ([leg.colorado.gov](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189)); Ogletree Deakins, "Colorado's New AI Act Targets Automated Decision-Making" ([ogletree.com](https://ogletree.com/insights-resources/blog-posts/colorados-new-ai-act-targets-automated-decision-making-for-consequential-decisions))

---

## Summary

- **NYC Local Law 144** is fully in effect and enforcement is expected to intensify significantly in 2026 following the Comptroller's damning audit. Employers using AEDTs should ensure bias audits are current and compliant.

- **Colorado SB 24-205** is dead — repealed, replaced, and its enforcement permanently stayed by a federal court. The replacement, **SB 26-189**, takes effect **January 1, 2027**, with a much narrower transparency-and-notice framework. No enforcement actions have occurred under either law to date, as the original never took effect and the replacement is not yet in force.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Here is my analysis:

---

## UK ICO vs. EDPB Guidance on AI and Data Protection: Comparison

### 1. Timing and Status of the Guidance

| | **UK ICO** | **EDPB** |
|---|---|---|
| **Key Document** | Outcome Report of the Generative AI Consultation Series (published **12 December 2024**) + ongoing updates to the "Guidance on AI and Data Protection" (last updated 15 March 2023, under review due to the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025) | **Opinion 28/2024** (adopted **17 December 2024**) on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models |
| **Legal Framework** | UK GDPR (assimilated Regulation (EU) 2016/679) — now diverging from EU GDPR due to the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 | EU GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) |

---

### 2. Key Areas of Alignment

Both regulators agree on several foundational points:

- **Legitimate interests as the primary lawful basis**: Both the ICO and EDPB conclude that legitimate interests (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR / UK GDPR) is the only viable lawful basis for training generative AI on web-scraped data, given that consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, and public task are generally inapplicable at scale.
- **Three-part test**: Both require the purpose test, necessity test, and balancing test to be satisfied.
- **Purpose specification**: Both insist that purposes must be *specifically defined* — vague formulations like "training AI models" are insufficient.
- **Data subject rights**: Both require AI models to be designed to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights (access, erasure, rectification, opt-out).
- **Case-by-case assessment of anonymisation**: Both reject the notion that AI models trained on personal data are automatically anonymous; this must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

---

### 3. Key Differences

#### A. Fairness Framework — ICO is More Granular and Prescriptive

The **ICO** has published a dedicated, stand-alone chapter on **"Fairness in AI"** within its AI and data protection guidance, along with **Annex A: Fairness in the AI lifecycle**. This includes:

- Detailed guidance on distinguishing **bias vs. discrimination** in the data protection context.
- Specific questions organisations should ask when considering fairness in automated decision-making under **Article 22 UK GDPR**.
- A lifecycle approach to fairness, addressing considerations at each stage of AI development and deployment.
- Explicit cross-referencing with the **UK Equality Act 2010**.

The **EDPB Opinion 28/2024**, by contrast, addresses fairness primarily through the lens of the balancing test within the legitimate interests assessment, without a comparable stand-alone fairness framework. The EDPB's approach is more procedural and less operationalised.

#### B. Statistical Accuracy vs. Data Protection Accuracy

The **ICO** draws an explicit distinction between **"statistical accuracy"** (a machine learning concept) and **"accuracy" as a data protection principle** under Article 5(1)(d). The ICO's guidance clarifies that AI systems do not need to be 100% statistically accurate to comply with the accuracy principle, but developers must be transparent about accuracy limitations and communicate them to downstream users.

The **EDPB** does not make this distinction as prominently. Its Opinion focuses more on the accuracy of *training data* and the risks of inaccurate outputs, without the same conceptual separation.

#### C. Legitimate Interests — ICO Emphasises Necessity More Stringently

The **ICO** places particular emphasis on the **necessity limb** of the three-part test. In its December 2024 Outcome Report, the ICO states that controllers must **"evidence why other available methods for data collection are not feasible"** — effectively requiring developers to demonstrate that less privacy-intrusive alternatives (e.g., synthetic data, curated datasets) are not viable before resorting to web scraping.

The **EDPB**, while also requiring necessity, frames it more in terms of whether the processing is *necessary for the purpose*, without the same explicit requirement to exhaust alternatives. The EDPB's approach is more focused on the balancing test and the **reasonable expectations of data subjects** as the decisive factor.

#### D. Data Subject Expectations — EDPB Assigns Greater Weight

The **EDPB** assigns **"significant weight"** to the reasonable expectations of data subjects in the balancing test. If personal data is processed for a purpose beyond what data subjects would reasonably expect at the time of collection, the EDPB indicates that fundamental rights could override the controller's interest. The EDPB also provides detailed guidance on **mitigating measures** (e.g., techniques short of full anonymisation that reduce identifiability).

The **ICO** addresses reasonable expectations too, but its framework is more focused on **transparency and purpose specification** as the mechanism for aligning with expectations, rather than treating expectations as a potentially overriding factor in the balancing test.

#### E. Consequences of Unlawful Processing — EDPB More Detailed

The **EDPB Opinion 28/2024** dedicates an entire section (Question 3/4) to the consequences of unlawful processing in the development phase on subsequent deployment. It confirms that:

- Unlawful initial processing *may* affect the lawfulness of subsequent deployment.
- Supervisory Authorities have **discretionary powers** to impose corrective measures, including fines, temporary limitations on processing, or erasure of unlawfully processed datasets.
- The EDPB provides a framework for assessing when a model developed with unlawfully processed data can still be lawfully deployed (e.g., if the controller can demonstrate that the unlawfulness has been remedied).

The **ICO** addresses this more through its general enforcement powers and its existing accountability framework, without the same structured analysis of downstream consequences.

#### F. Practical Guidance — ICO Provides More Operational Detail

The **ICO** provides concrete, operational examples including:

- Granting a **reasonable period** between data collection and use to enable rights exercise.
- Implementing **mechanisms to alert controllers** of unauthorised personal data outputs (to enable "unlearning").
- Specific guidance on **inferences, affinity groups, and special category data**.
- A dedicated chapter on **transparency and explainability** (linked to the separate "Explaining Decisions Made with AI" guidance).

The **EDPB Opinion** is more high-level and directed at **supervisory authorities** as much as at controllers, providing a framework for DPAs to assess compliance rather than operational playbooks for organisations.

#### G. Regulatory Divergence — The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025

A critical structural difference: the **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025**, which received Royal Assent on **19 June 2025**, means the ICO's guidance is now under active review and will evolve under a distinct UK legal framework that diverges from EU GDPR. The ICO has explicitly flagged that its AI guidance "may be subject to change." The EDPB's guidance remains anchored in the EU GDPR, which is not subject to the same legislative reform.

---

### 4. Summary Table

| Issue | **ICO Position** | **EDPB Position** |
|---|---|---|
| Lawful basis for web scraping | Legitimate interests only; strict necessity test | Legitimate interests; emphasis on balancing test and data subject expectations |
| Fairness | Dedicated chapter + lifecycle annex; operational guidance | Addressed within balancing test; less granular |
| Accuracy | Explicit distinction between statistical accuracy and DP accuracy | Less conceptual separation |
| Necessity | Must evidence why alternatives are not feasible | Necessity assessed within three-part test; less emphasis on exhausting alternatives |
| Data subject expectations | Addressed via transparency and purpose specification | Given "significant weight" in balancing test; can override controller interests |
| Consequences of unlawful processing | General enforcement framework | Detailed structured analysis; SA discretion framework |
| Practical operational guidance | Extensive (unlearning, opt-out mechanisms, timing windows) | More high-level; directed at DPAs |
| Regulatory trajectory | Under review due to Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 — likely further divergence | Stable within EU GDPR framework |

---

### 5. Practical Implications

Organisations operating in both the UK and EU should:

1. **Map to the stricter standard**: Where the ICO is more prescriptive (e.g., fairness lifecycle, necessity evidence), comply with the higher bar across both regimes.
2. **Document the three-part test separately**: The ICO's emphasis on evidencing why alternatives are not feasible requires distinct documentation from the EDPB's expectation-focused balancing test.
3. **Monitor the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025**: The ICO's guidance is flagged for revision; expect further divergence from the EDPB position as UK-specific secondary legislation and ICO guidance emerge post-June 2025.
4. **Implement operational measures**: The ICO's practical recommendations (unlearning mechanisms, opt-out windows, accuracy communication to downstream users) represent emerging best practice that EU regulators are likely to look to as well.

Here is a comprehensive overview of recent SEC enforcement actions and staff guidance addressing model governance and AI use in trading, advisory, and disclosure contexts.

---

## I. Enforcement Actions

### A. Two Sigma Investments — Model Governance Failures (January 2025)

The most significant model governance enforcement action to date. On **January 16, 2025**, the SEC announced settled charges against Two Sigma Investments LP and Two Sigma Advisers LP for:

- **Failing to address known vulnerabilities** in their algorithmic trading models, breaching their fiduciary duty of care.
- **Deficient policies and procedures** — the firm lacked written policies to prevent model-related violations.
- **Supervisory failures** — an employee made unauthorized changes to investment models that went undetected.
- **Whistleblower protection rule violations.**

**Penalty:** $90 million in SEC penalties; Two Sigma also repaid $165 million to affected clients.

> **Source:** [SEC Press Release 2025-15](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-15) (Jan. 16, 2025); *In the Matter of Two Sigma Investments, LP*, SEC Release No. 102207.

### B. Jian Wu — Model Manipulation (September 2025)

On **September 11, 2025**, the SEC and DOJ brought parallel criminal and civil actions against Jian Wu, a former senior quantitative researcher at Two Sigma. Wu allegedly:

- Manipulated algorithmic trading models **14 times** between November 2021 and August 2023.
- Funneled **$23.5 million** in improper compensation to himself.
- Caused at least **$165 million in losses** to client funds and accounts.

This case underscores that model governance must extend to **insider threat detection** and access controls over production models.

> **Source:** [SEC Litigation Release LR-26398](https://www.sec.gov/enforcement-litigation/litigation-releases/lr-26398) (Sept. 11, 2025).

### C. AI-Washing Enforcement Actions (2024–2025)

The SEC has aggressively pursued firms making false or misleading claims about AI capabilities:

| Date | Entity | Allegation | Penalty |
|------|--------|------------|---------|
| **March 18, 2024** | Delphia (USA) Inc. | False/misleading statements about AI use in SEC filings, press releases, and website | $225,000 |
| **March 18, 2024** | Global Predictions, Inc. | False/misleading AI claims; Marketing Rule violations | $175,000 |
| **April 9, 2025** | Albert Saniger (CEO, Nate Inc.) | Materially false statements to investors about AI capabilities; parallel SEC + SDNY criminal action | Pending |
| **April 22, 2025** | Additional AI-washing action (SEC + EDNY) | False AI capability claims | Pending |

These were the **first-ever SEC enforcement actions explicitly targeting "AI-washing"** under the Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1 under the Advisers Act).

> **Sources:** [Mayer Brown — First AI-Washing Enforcement Actions](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2024/04/securities-and-exchange-commission-brings-first-enforcement-actions-over-aiwashing); [Debevoise — SEC and DOJ Continued Focus on AI Washing](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/2025/04/17/the-sec-and-doj-signal-continued-focus-on-ai-washing-under-trump-administration).

---

## II. Rulemaking: Predictive Data Analytics Conflicts Rule (Finalized June 2025)

On **June 12, 2025**, the SEC issued its **final rule** on **Conflicts of Interest Associated with the Use of Predictive Data Analytics** (File No. S7-12-23; Release Nos. 33-11377, 34-103247, IA-6885, IC-35635). Key requirements:

- Broker-dealers and investment advisers must **evaluate and identify conflicts of interest** arising from their use of predictive data analytics and AI in investor interactions.
- Firms must **document and address** any conflicts identified.
- The rule is technology-neutral but directly targets AI-driven recommendation and advisory tools.

> **Source:** [SEC Final Rule — Conflicts of Interest / Predictive Data Analytics](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/2025/06/s7-12-23).

---

## III. SEC Division of Examinations — 2025 Priorities

The **2025 Examination Priorities** (published October 2024) signal a significant escalation in AI scrutiny. Examiners will assess:

1. **Accuracy of AI representations** — whether firms' public claims about AI capabilities match reality.
2. **Policies and procedures** — whether registrants have adequate policies to monitor and supervise AI use in:
   - Fraud prevention and detection
   - Back-office operations
   - Anti-money laundering (AML)
   - **Trading functions**
3. **Third-party AI models** — how firms protect against loss or misuse of client records when using vendor AI tools.
4. **Automation of internal processes** — whether automated decision-making is appropriately governed.

> **Source:** [Mayer Brown — SEC 2025 Exam Priorities](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2024/11/sec-division-of-examinations-announces-2025-exam-priorities); [Morgan Lewis — 2025 Exam Priorities](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2024/10/compliance-alert-secs-2025-examination-priorities).

---

## IV. AI Disclosure Guidance — Ongoing Developments

- **March 6, 2025:** The SEC's **Investment Advisory Committee** held a panel titled *"Disclosure of Artificial Intelligence's Impact on Operations,"* examining whether the SEC should create a dedicated AI disclosure framework.
- **Ongoing (2025–2026):** Public companies continue to seek SEC guidance on what AI activities and risks are material and must be disclosed. The SEC has signaled that existing disclosure rules (e.g., MD&A, risk factors) already apply to material AI risks, and that **AI-washing in public filings** may lead to fraud claims under the federal securities laws.
- The SEC has been urged to issue formal **"Disclosure Guidance"** clarifying how existing rules apply to AI, analogous to the 2023 cybersecurity incident reporting rule.

---

## V. Cross-Reference: SR 11-7 (Model Risk Management Guidance)

While SR 11-7 is banking agency guidance (OCC, Fed, FDIC), its principles are increasingly referenced in SEC contexts. The **April 17, 2026 revision** to SR 11-7 explicitly notes that generative AI and agentic AI models are **not within scope**, but emphasizes that a firm's "risk management and governance practices should guide the determination of appropriate governance and controls for any tools, processes, or systems not covered." The core SR 11-7 principles — model inventory, validation, ongoing monitoring, clear roles and responsibilities, and vendor model oversight — align closely with what the SEC expects of registrants using AI in trading and advisory functions.

| **Disclosure** | IAC panel on AI disclosure; ongoing calls for SEC guidance | Mar 2025–ongoing |

The clear trajectory is that the SEC expects **robust model governance, accurate AI disclosures, documented conflict evaluations, and meaningful policies and procedures** — and is willing to bring significant enforcement actions where firms fall short.

reflected in this guidance, model risk management practices vary from banking organization to

that process. The nature and sophistication of a banking organization’s model governance is

complexity of the organization.

Model risk management benefits from clear roles and responsibilities with well-defined 
accountability, including with respect to potential conflicts of interest (e.g., misalignment of 
incentives between different reporting lines, such as model development and validation groups).

the model lifecycle, from development through validation and ongoing monitoring. In cases 
where internal audit is part of the banking organization’s model risk management practices, 
internal audit would generally not duplicate model risk management activities such as model 
development or validation. Instead, internal audit’s role is generally to evaluate whether the

## Most Recent FDA Guidance on AI/ML-Enabled Medical Devices

The most recent FDA guidance is the **Draft Guidance: "Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations"** (Docket No. FDA-2024-D-4488), published on **January 6–7, 2025**. This is a draft guidance — not yet final — with public comments accepted through **April 7, 2025**.

### Key Provisions of the FDA Draft Guidance

The guidance adopts a **Total Product Lifecycle (TPLC)** approach and centers on four pillars:

1. **Lifecycle Management & Performance Monitoring**: Manufacturers should describe postmarket performance monitoring plans in their marketing submissions. This includes continuous monitoring of AI model performance across the device's entire lifespan, with mechanisms to detect drift, degradation, or emergent bias.

2. **Transparency**: Detailed strategies to improve user understanding of AI outputs, including recommended demographic analyses and postmarket reporting on model behavior across subpopulations.

3. **Bias Mitigation**: Specific recommendations for identifying, measuring, and mitigating bias throughout development, validation, and postmarket phases.

4. **Change Management (PCCPs)**: The guidance builds on the FDA's earlier PCCP framework (finalized in December 2024), which allows manufacturers to pre-specify planned modifications to AI-enabled devices and the methodology for validating them — enabling iterative improvement **without requiring new marketing submissions** for each update, so long as changes stay within the approved PCCP boundaries.

The FDA is also specifically seeking comment on how the guidance aligns with the AI lifecycle, its adequacy for generative AI, and the approach to performance monitoring as a risk mitigation tool.

---

## EU AI Act High-Risk Classification for Medical AI

### The Classification Trigger: Article 6 and Annex I

Under the **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)**, an AI system is classified as **high-risk** via two routes:

- **Article 6(1)**: The AI system is (a) intended to be used as a **safety component** of a product, or **is itself a product**, covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in **Annex I**, **and** (b) the product is required to undergo a **third-party conformity assessment** (i.e., Notified Body review) under that legislation.

- **Article 6(2)**: The AI system falls within one of the use cases listed in **Annex III** (e.g., biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment).

For medical devices, the key legislation in **Annex I, Section A** is the **EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) 2017/745** and the **In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) 2017/746**. This means:

- **Class IIa, IIb, and III medical devices** (which require Notified Body involvement under the MDR) that incorporate AI are **automatically high-risk** under Article 6(1).
- **Class I medical devices** (which generally do not require Notified Body review) are **not** classified as high-risk under Article 6(1), though they could still be caught under Article 6(2) / Annex III in certain circumstances.

### Obligations for High-Risk Medical AI

Once classified as high-risk, providers must comply with the requirements in **Chapter III, Section 2** of the AI Act, including:

| Requirement | Article |
|---|---|
| Risk Management System (continuous, iterative, lifecycle-wide) | Art. 9 |
| Data Governance (training, validation, testing data quality) | Art. 10 |
| Technical Documentation (drawn up before market placement) | Art. 11 & Annex IV |
| Transparency & Instructions for Use | Art. 13 |
| Human Oversight | Art. 14 |
| Accuracy, Robustness & Cybersecurity | Art. 15 |
| Quality Management System | Art. 17 |
| Conformity Assessment & CE Marking | Arts. 43, 47, 48 |
| Post-Market Monitoring | Art. 72 |
| Serious Incident Reporting | Art. 73 |

---

## Interaction Between the Two Frameworks

### 1. Dual Compliance Model (EU)

The **MDCG 2025-6 / AIB 2025-1 guidance** (published June 2025) clarifies that AI-enabled medical devices ("MDAI") must comply with **both** the MDR/IVDR and the AI Act. This is a **dual compliance model** — the AI Act does not replace MDR requirements but adds a new layer. Key operational points:

- **Single technical documentation** can satisfy both frameworks where requirements overlap (Art. 11(2) AI Act).
- **Single conformity assessment** is possible: for Article 6(1) devices, the MDR/IVDR conformity assessment procedure applies, with AI Act requirements integrated.
- **Full enforcement** of the AI Act for high-risk medical devices begins **August 2027** (36-month transition from the August 2024 entry into force).

### 2. Change Management: The Critical Divergence

This is where the two frameworks differ most sharply:

| Dimension | FDA (PCCP) | EU AI Act |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-approved changes** | Yes — PCCP allows pre-specified modifications without new submissions | Limited — changes pre-determined at initial conformity assessment are permitted, but "substantial modifications" require re-certification |
| **Definition of "substantial"** | Defined by PCCP scope; objective criteria | Art. 3(23): any change not foreseen in the initial conformity assessment that affects compliance or modifies intended purpose — **less objective** than FDA |
| **Update timeline** | Weeks (within approved PCCP) | 3–6 months (Notified Body review) |
| **Philosophy** | Iterative, agile, innovation-friendly | Precautionary, certification-heavy |

### 3. Areas of Alignment

Despite the divergence in change management philosophy, the two frameworks converge on several core expectations:

- **Lifecycle-wide risk management**: Both require continuous, iterative risk management (FDA TPLC approach ↔ EU AI Act Art. 9).
- **Post-market monitoring**: Both mandate systematic postmarket surveillance and performance monitoring (FDA performance monitoring plans ↔ EU AI Act Art. 72).
- **Transparency**: Both emphasize clear instructions for use and interpretability of AI outputs (FDA transparency recommendations ↔ EU AI Act Art. 13).
- **Bias mitigation**: Both frameworks now explicitly address bias as a safety and effectiveness concern.
- **Technical documentation**: Both require comprehensive documentation demonstrating safety and performance.

### 4. Practical Implications for Manufacturers

A manufacturer seeking to market an AI-enabled medical device in **both** the US and EU must:

- Prepare **unified but dual-purpose technical documentation** that satisfies both FDA marketing submission requirements and the EU AI Act's Annex IV.
- Design a **risk management system** (e.g., ISO 14971-aligned) that addresses both FDA's TPLC expectations and the AI Act's Art. 9 requirements.
- Navigate the **PCCP vs. substantial modification** tension: a change that is safely within a PCCP for FDA purposes may still trigger re-certification in the EU if it affects AI Act compliance or intended purpose.
- Plan for **staggered timelines**: FDA guidance is still in draft (comments through April 2025), while EU AI Act obligations for high-risk devices phase in through August 2027.

### 5. Notable Development: Potential EU Simplification

It is worth noting that the **European Commission** has signaled a potential **radical simplification**: moving the MDR/IVDR from Annex I, Section A to Section B of the AI Act. If enacted, this would largely exempt medical devices from the AI Act's scope (per Art. 2(2)), on the theory that the MDR/IVDR already provide adequate protection. This proposal is under discussion and not yet adopted, but it could fundamentally alter the dual-compliance landscape.

---

**Bottom line**: The FDA's January 2025 draft guidance and the EU AI Act both embrace lifecycle-oriented regulation of AI/ML medical devices, but they diverge sharply on change management — the FDA's PCCP mechanism enables agile, pre-approved iteration, while the EU AI Act's "substantial modification" trigger imposes a more rigid re-certification burden. Manufacturers targeting both markets should build unified quality and documentation systems while planning for the asymmetric impact of AI model updates across jurisdictions.

**Article 9: Risk Management System**
### Article 9: Risk Management System

1. A risk management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained in relation to high-risk AI systems.

2. The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating. It shall comprise the following steps:

(a) the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose;

(b) the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse;

(c) the evaluation of other risks possibly arising, based on the analysis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72;

(d) the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified pursuant to point (a).

3. The risks referred to in this Article shall concern only those which may be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or the provision of adequate technical information.

4. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall give due consideration to the effects and possible interaction resulting from the combined application of the requirements set out in this Section, with a view to minimising risks more effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures to fulfil those requirements.

5. The risk management measures referred to in paragraph 2, point (d), shall be such that the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable. In identifying the most appropriate risk management measures, the following shall be ensured:

(a) elimination or reduction of risks identified and evaluated pursuant to paragraph 2 in as far as technically feasible through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system;

(b) where appropriate, implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that cannot be eliminated;

(c) provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

**Article 17: Quality Management System**
### Article 17: Quality Management System

1. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall put a quality management system in place that ensures compliance with this Regulation. That system shall be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions, and shall include at least the following aspects:

(a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system;

(b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the design, design control and design verification of the high-risk AI system;

(c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system;

(d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency with which they have to be carried out;

(e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all of the relevant requirements set out in Section 2, the means to be used to ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with those requirements;

(f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention and any other operation regarding the data that is performed before and for the purpose of the placing on the market or the putting into service of high-risk AI systems;

(g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9;

(h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system, in accordance with Article 72;

(i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73;

(j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, including those providing or supporting the access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties;

(k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information;

(l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures;

(m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of the management and other staff with regard to all the aspects listed in this paragraph.

**Article 8: Compliance with the Requirements**
### Article 8: Compliance with the Requirements

1. High-risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in this Section, taking into account their intended purpose as well as the generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI-related technologies. The risk management system referred to in Article 9 shall be taken into account when ensuring compliance with those requirements.

2. Where a product contains an AI system, to which the requirements of this Regulation as well as requirements of the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I apply, providers shall be responsible for ensuring that their product is fully compliant with all applicable requirements under applicable Union harmonisation legislation. In ensuring the compliance of high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1 with the requirements set out in this Section, and in order to ensure consistency, avoid duplication and minimise additional burdens, providers shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary testing and reporting processes, information and documentation they provide with regard to their product into documentation and procedures that already exist and are required under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I.

**Article 13: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers**
### Article 13: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. An appropriate type and degree of transparency shall be ensured with a view to achieving compliance with the relevant obligations of the provider and deployer set out in Section 3.

2. High-risk AI systems shall be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise that include concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers.

(a) the identity and the contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative;

(b) the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the high-risk AI system, including:

(i) its intended purpose;

(ii) the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the high-risk AI system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, and any known and foreseeable circumstances that may have an impact on that expected level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity;

(iii) any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to the health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2);

(iv) where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the high-risk AI system to provide information that is relevant to explain its output;

(v) when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used;

### Article 11: Technical Documentation

1. The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date. It shall contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV. SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner.
